# 0. Purpose of this notebook

The four registered predictions about the ratings are tested in the ratings
analysis, `Study1_01_Quant.Rmd`. This notebook re-estimates none of them and
gives no verdict on any of them. Two of the four concern the level of the
ratings: whether attributing the work to an image generator lowers them on
both dimensions, and whether that reduction is larger for effort than for
creativity. The third asks whether the reduction differs between figurative
and non-figurative images, and it predicts no difference. A prediction of no
difference is decided by an equivalence test, a procedure that asks whether
an estimate sits inside a stated bound rather than whether it differs from
zero. The registered bound is ±0.20 rating points, and the prediction is
decided only when two random-effects structures agree. The random effects
are the terms that give each participant and each image its own baseline or
its own effect. The intercepts-only structure gives each a baseline; the
maximal structure adds the random slopes the design allows, letting an
effect vary from one participant or image to the next. The fourth
prediction, tested in `Study1_01_Quant.Rmd` section 7.8, asks whether
attribution changes what a rating is a property of, with the variance
between participants rising and the variance within a participant, from
image to image, falling. Its verdict is read there rather than restated
here. Wherever this notebook needs one of those results as background, it
points to the file that tests it.

Each participant wrote a short justification beside every rating. Section
2.4 reports how long those justifications run and how often each measure
fires. A companion notebook, `Study1_02_Text.ipynb`, reads the
justifications, applies a fixed set of search patterns to them, and records
for each response a true/false or three-way flag for each pattern. **This
file joins those flags back to the ratings and runs the statistics.** Every
model in the text program is fitted here, not in the notebook.

The file asks three questions of the justifications.

1. **What did people mean by "effort"?** In the human-attribution arm, is
   effort talk about visible detail in the picture, about time and
   industriousness, or about skill? The paper maps the effort rating onto the
   "sweat of the brow" standard, under which labour alone earns copyright, and
   which *Feist v. Rural Telephone* rejected. That mapping assumes an answer
   to this question, so the answer is measured here rather than assumed.
   Section 3.

2. **What did people mean by "creativity"?** The same question, asked of the
   other rating. In the human-attribution arm, was creativity talk about the
   *concept* (the idea, meaning, thought or story behind the work), about
   *novelty* (whether the work looked new or looked familiar), or about
   *execution* (the visible detail and rendering)? Doctrinally this question
   matters most. Creativity is the criterion *Feist v. Rural Telephone* kept,
   and effort is the criterion it set aside, so whatever "creativity" denoted
   for these raters is what the protected quantity was measured as. The
   novelty component carries a second point of its own. Novelty, in the sense
   of "not previously known to the world", is a *patent* requirement, not a
   copyright one. Copyright asks only for independent creation plus a minimal
   spark of creativity, so two people who independently paint the same sunset
   each own their own painting. If lay raters lower the creativity score for
   work that strikes them as familiar, derivative or generic, they are
   importing a test that copyright law rejects. Section 4 asks this
   denotation question (what the word picked out for the people who used it)
   together with its three components.

3. **What did the human-arm participants write about machines?** All ten
   images were machine-generated, so the human-attribution arm was given a
   cover story: its vignette, the description of the artist shown to that
   arm, said a person made them. The instrument has no manipulation check (no
   question asked participants who they thought made the work), so the only
   audit of the cover story is a count of the human-arm participants who
   brought a machine into their explanations unprompted. Section 5 reports
   that count twice, from two fixed search patterns. The broad count is of
   participants whose writing mentions machines or prompting at all. The
   narrow count is of participants who state that the work is or looks
   machine-made. That count comes from the machine-authorship rule, with the
   negated and conditional sentences ("it doesn't look AI generated", "if a
   computer made this") set aside. Neither count measures disbelief. A person can doubt
   the vignette and write nothing about it, and a person can say a picture
   looks machine-made while accepting what they were told. Each count comes
   with an interval from resampling participants, that is, from recomputing
   the count on many samples of participants drawn with replacement from the
   real ones. The section then refits the primary models on both dimensions
   without the participants in the narrow count. Beside that refit it puts a
   matched removal: the effect size recomputed after removing random groups of
   the same size with nearly the same average effort rating, which shows how
   far such a removal moves it for arithmetic reasons alone.

Questions 1 and 2 each end in a registered comparison, not in a pair of rates
set side by side. The preregistration (section 9 of that document) names five
directional tests over these texts: visible detail against time and against
skill in the human arm's effort explanations, concept against execution and
against novelty in the human arm's creativity explanations, and prompting
talk across the machine arm's two rating dimensions. All five use the same
model, a mixed logistic regression: a regression for a true-or-false outcome
that gives each participant and each image its own baseline, so that twenty
explanations from one person are not counted as twenty independent
observations. The four denotation comparisons sit in sections 3 and 4,
beside the rates they decide, and the fifth sits in section 6. Section 7
corrects the five p-values together for the number of tests, treating them
as the one exploratory family the preregistration declares. They are kept
apart from the confirmatory family, the four registered tests that
`Study1_01_Quant.Rmd` corrects together.

Section 6 also reports how often participants in each arm talked about
prompting at all. Question 3's count is read against that scale.

Section 8 stands apart from the three questions. It runs two checks that are
the same in every study of this program where a rating exists. The first asks
how closely the words alone track the rating and the arm. As a registered
descriptive quantity, it belongs to no correction family. The second asks
whether participants told a machine made the works reuse their own words
across the ten images more than participants told a person did. It carries a
predicted direction, and its two dimensions are corrected together by the
Holm procedure: the smaller p-value is compared against half the usual .05
threshold and, only if it passes, the larger against .05. Each check is
reported whatever it shows. Section 9 is a general description of the
explanations, also run in every study, and gives no verdicts. It covers the
emotional tone and concreteness of the words people chose, the topics their
explanations fall into, and the words a model relies on when it predicts the
arm or the rating. Section 10 draws the three figures. Section 11 records
what this run read and wrote and the exact software environment. Section 12
lists approaches that were tried and set aside.

**How measurement works in this program.** Every measure in sections 3 to 8
is written down in advance and applied identically to every response. The
flags of sections 3 to 7 are search patterns, and section 8 works from counts
of content words (the words left once function words such as "the" and "of"
are removed). Nothing judges an individual response, neither a language
model nor a human coder. Researcher judgment enters once, in the rules. The
rules are printed in full in `tables/text_rules.txt`, and the responses they
matched are listed in `tables/text_audit_matches.txt`. Section 9 adds two
descriptions that are not search patterns but are just as fixed. One uses
published word norms: the average ratings that large samples of people gave
single English words for how pleasant, how calm or excited, how in control
and how concrete each word feels, collected by other laboratories before this
study existed. The other is a topic model, a method that finds groups of
words that tend to occur together and describes each explanation as a mix of
those groups. Its settings and its number of groups are fixed by rules
written into the notebook's code. The notebook computes all of these without
seeing the arm or the rating, and this file is where the arm and the rating
are joined back.

# 1. Setup

## 1.1 Packages

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The same packages as Study1_01_Quant.Rmd, minus the ones that file needs
# only for its ordinal and diagnostic models. Each package carries a comment
# saying what it is used for here.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # pipes, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr
library(here)        # path handling that survives working-directory changes
library(janitor)     # clean_names(), tabyl(), adorn_*() for quick crosstabs

# Mixed-effects models. A mixed-effects model is a regression that allows for
# observations that are not independent: each participant contributed 20
# responses, and each image was rated by all 111 people. lme4 fits the
# models. lmerTest wraps lme4 so that summary() and anova() report p-values
# whose degrees of freedom come from the Satterthwaite approximation, which
# estimates them from the model's variance components. Psychology papers
# usually report these, and Study1_01_Quant.Rmd does too, so the two files
# agree.
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

# emmeans computes estimated marginal means, the model's predicted average
# for each group with the other predictors held at neutral values, and the
# contrasts between them.
library(emmeans)

# broom and broom.mixed turn model objects into tidy data frames, one row per
# coefficient, which can be written straight to CSV.
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)

# Visualization. patchwork composes multi-panel figures; scales formats axes.
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

# glmnet fits the ridge regressions in section 8.1: regressions of the rating,
# and of the arm, on several hundred word counts at once, with a penalty that
# shrinks every coefficient toward zero so that a model with more predictors
# than it has information to support does not simply memorise the training
# responses. Section 9.3 uses the same package for the lasso, the version of
# that penalty that sets most coefficients to exactly zero and so names the
# few words a prediction rests on. The AUC of section 8.1, a measure of how
# well a score separates the two arms, is computed by hand from the rank
# formula, not with the pROC package, so pROC is not loaded.
library(glmnet)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reproducibility. The resampled intervals in this file are built from random
# draws, so the seed fixes them: with another seed, the third decimal place of
# those intervals can move. Study1_01_Quant.Rmd uses the same seed.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(20260421)
```

#           └── Final Paper/              <- manuscript + paper-ready outputs
#
# PROJECT_ROOT below is found from this file's own folder, which is the
# working directory when the file is knitted: it is the first folder at or
# above it that holds both Data and Analysis. Where the file runs from
# somewhere else, as on a Colab runtime, setting the environment variable
# STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT gives the root instead, so the same file runs unchanged
# in both places. Every other path is built from it. The path contains
# spaces, which R handles as long as paths are built with file.path() and
# not by pasting strings together.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PROJECT_ROOT <- local({
  is_root <- function(p) dir.exists(file.path(p, "Data")) &&
                         dir.exists(file.path(p, "Analysis"))
  root <- Sys.getenv("STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT")
  if (nzchar(root)) {
    root <- normalizePath(root, mustWork = FALSE)
    if (!is_root(root)) {
      stop("The folder STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT names has no Data and Analysis ",
           "folders.")
    }
  } else {
    root <- normalizePath(getwd(), mustWork = TRUE)
    while (!is_root(root)) {
      if (identical(dirname(root), root)) {
        stop("No folder at or above the working directory holds both Data ",
             "and Analysis. Knit this file from its own folder, or set ",
             "STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT to the project root.")
      }
      root <- dirname(root)
    }
  }
  root
})

## 1.3 A guard so that a broken model is reported, not silently skipped

```{r run-or-report}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every model and every resampling routine below is wrapped in this helper.
#
# The failure it prevents runs as follows. A model fails to converge, the
# chunk errors, and the knit (the run that renders this file to a report)
# stops halfway. Someone adds error = TRUE to the chunk header to get past it.
# The model then disappears without notice, and the manuscript keeps citing a
# number from the last run that worked. run_or_report() catches the failure,
# prints it, records it in a log that is written to disk at the end, and
# returns NULL so that later code can check for it. A step's status is "ok"
# or "error".
#
# Usage: run_or_report("label", function() { ... })
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

MODEL_LOG <- tibble(
  step    = character(),
  status  = character(),
  message = character()
)

run_or_report <- function(label, f) {
  status <- "ok"
  msg    <- ""
  value  <- tryCatch(
    f(),
    error = function(e) {
      status <<- "error"
      msg    <<- conditionMessage(e)
      NULL
    }
  )
  MODEL_LOG <<- bind_rows(
    MODEL_LOG,
    tibble(step = label, status = status, message = msg)
  )
  if (status == "error") {
    cat("\n!! STEP FAILED: ", label, "\n   ", msg, "\n\n", sep = "")
  }
  value
}

# Small formatting helper used throughout: turn a proportion into a percentage
# string with one decimal place.
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A STATUS FOR EVERY MODEL FIT, AND WHAT A STATUS PERMITS.
#
# A step can finish while the model inside it did not. lme4 can hand back a
# fit whose optimiser (the routine that searches for the best parameter
# values) stopped on a slope, or a fit with a variance pushed to zero, and
# both look like ordinary numbers in a table. So every mixed model in
# this file goes through fit_mixed(), which keeps the fit, keeps everything
# lme4 said while fitting it, and gives it one of four statuses:
#
#   ok              the fit finished with no warning from the optimiser or
#                   from lme4, and is not singular.
#   singular        the fit finished cleanly but sits on the boundary: a
#                   random-effect variance estimated at zero, or a correlation
#                   at plus or minus one. The fixed effects (the
#                   coefficients the tables report) are still estimated, so
#                   a singular fit keeps its p-value, and the status says
#                   where the boundary is.
#   nonconvergence  some warning was still standing after one restart: the
#                   optimiser stopped where the likelihood was still sloping,
#                   the curvature at the stopping point could not be computed,
#                   or lme4 raised any other complaint. Standard errors from
#                   such a fit cannot be trusted.
#   error           there is no fit at all.
#
# Only ok and singular fits (ELIGIBLE_STATUS) may carry a p-value, an
# interval, a Benjamini-Hochberg value (a p-value corrected for the number of
# tests, section 7.1) or a verdict. For the other two the
# estimate is kept where one exists, every inferential column is NA, and the
# note column says why. Every fit is also written, with its status and
# note, to FIT_LOG, which section 11.1 deposits beside MODEL_LOG.
#
# HOW A FIT IS RUN, AND WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE OPTIMISER STOPS SHORT.
#
# The optimiser is bobyqa, the same one every mixed model in this file uses.
# An optimiser searches for the parameter values that make the data most
# likely, and it stops when its steps become small enough; occasionally it
# stops while the likelihood surface is still sloping, which lme4 reports as
# "failed to converge with max|grad| = ...", the gradient (the slope at the
# stopping point) being larger than lme4 tolerates. The remedy lme4's own
# troubleshooting page gives is to start the same optimiser again from where
# it stopped, with a larger budget of function evaluations. That is done
# here, once, when the first pass raised any warning other than a singular
# fit. Whether a restart happened, what the first pass said, and whether the
# restart cleared it all go into the note, so the table carries the full
# history of the fit rather than only its final state.
#
# Warnings are caught by a calling handler, a hook that sees each warning as
# it is raised and then lets the fit continue. The fit is kept and the
# warning is kept, which a plain tryCatch cannot do (it would abandon the fit
# at the first warning). lme4's own convergence record
# (fit@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages) is read as well, because it is the
# authoritative version of the same information.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

ELIGIBLE_STATUS <- c("ok", "singular")

FIT_LOG <- tibble(
  step   = character(),
  model  = character(),
  status = character(),
  note   = character()
)

# Where a singular fit sits on the boundary, in words.
describe_singular <- function(fit) {
  vc  <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(fit))
  out <- character()
  vars <- vc[is.na(vc$var2) & vc$grp != "Residual", , drop = FALSE]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(vars))) {
    if (vars$vcov[i] < 1e-8) {
      out <- c(out, if (vars$var1[i] == "(Intercept)") {
        paste0("the random-intercept variance for ", vars$grp[i],
               " was estimated at exactly zero")
      } else {
        paste0("the variance of the ", vars$var1[i], " slope for ",
               vars$grp[i], " was estimated at exactly zero")
      })
    }
  }
  cors <- vc[!is.na(vc$var2), , drop = FALSE]
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cors))) {
    if (abs(cors$sdcor[i]) > 1 - 1e-6) {
      out <- c(out, paste0("the correlation between ", cors$var1[i], " and ",
                           cors$var2[i], " for ", cors$grp[i],
                           " was estimated at ", sprintf("%+.0f", cors$sdcor[i])))
    }
  }
  if (length(out) == 0) out <- "a random-effect parameter sits on its boundary"
  paste0("singular fit: ", paste(out, collapse = " and "))
}

# One mixed model, with its status. `family = NULL` fits a linear mixed model
# with lmerTest (so summary() carries Satterthwaite p-values); a family fits
# a generalized one with lme4::glmer. Returns list(fit, status, note).
fit_mixed <- function(formula, data, family = NULL, step = "",
                      REML = TRUE) {
  is_glmm <- !is.null(family)

  one_pass <- function(start = NULL, maxfun = NULL) {
    opt_ctrl <- if (is.null(maxfun)) list() else list(maxfun = maxfun)
    msgs <- character()
    fit  <- withCallingHandlers(
      tryCatch(
        if (is_glmm) {
          lme4::glmer(formula, data = data, family = family,
                      control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                                             optCtrl = opt_ctrl),
                      start = start)
        } else {
          lmerTest::lmer(formula, data = data, REML = REML,
                         control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                                               optCtrl = opt_ctrl),
                         start = start)
        },
        error = function(e) {
          msgs <<- c(msgs, paste0("error: ", conditionMessage(e)))
          NULL
        }
      ),
      warning = function(w) {
        msgs <<- c(msgs, trimws(conditionMessage(w)))
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      },
      message = function(m) {
        msgs <<- c(msgs, trimws(conditionMessage(m)))
        invokeRestart("muffleMessage")
      }
    )
    if (!is.null(fit)) {
      msgs <- c(msgs, fit@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages)
    }
    # lme4 announces a singular fit as a message too; that is reported
    # separately, in plainer words, so it is set aside here. The optimiser
    # messages carry a pointer to the help pages; the note keeps the
    # substance and drops the pointer.
    msgs <- unique(msgs[!grepl("singular", msgs, ignore.case = TRUE)])
    msgs <- trimws(sub("\\s*See \\?lme4::convergence.*$", "", msgs))
    list(fit = fit, msgs = msgs[nzchar(msgs)])
  }

  first  <- one_pass()
  fit    <- first$fit
  notes  <- first$msgs
  status <- if (is.null(fit)) "error" else "ok"

  if (!is.null(fit) && length(first$msgs) > 0) {
    start  <- if (is_glmm) {
      list(theta = lme4::getME(fit, "theta"), fixef = lme4::fixef(fit))
    } else {
      list(theta = lme4::getME(fit, "theta"))
    }
    second <- one_pass(start = start, maxfun = 2e5)
    if (!is.null(second$fit)) {
      fit   <- second$fit
      notes <- c(
        paste0("first bobyqa pass stopped short (",
               paste(first$msgs, collapse = "; "),
               "); refitted with bobyqa from that end point with maxfun = ",
               "200000"),
        if (length(second$msgs) == 0) "restart converged"
        else paste0("restart still reported: ",
                    paste(second$msgs, collapse = "; "))
      )
      if (length(second$msgs) > 0) status <- "nonconvergence"
    } else {
      notes  <- c(notes, paste0("restart from the first pass failed (",
                                paste(second$msgs, collapse = "; "),
                                "); the first-pass fit is kept"))
      status <- "nonconvergence"
    }
  } else if (!is.null(fit)) {
    notes <- c("converged", notes)
  }

  if (!is.null(fit) && status == "ok") {
    if (lme4::isSingular(fit)) {
      status <- "singular"
      notes  <- c(notes, describe_singular(fit))
    } else {
      notes  <- c(notes, "not singular")
    }
  }

  note <- paste0("status ", status, "; ", paste(notes, collapse = "; "))
  FIT_LOG <<- bind_rows(FIT_LOG, tibble(
    step   = step,
    model  = paste(deparse(formula, width.cutoff = 500L), collapse = " "),
    status = status,
    note   = note
  ))
  list(fit = fit, status = status, note = note)
}

# The fixed effects of a linear mixed model as a tidy table, with the status
# and note beside them and every inferential column emptied when the status
# does not permit inference. A fit that does not exist gives one row with
# empty numbers, so a table built from several fits keeps a row for it.
tidy_mixed <- function(res) {
  if (is.null(res$fit)) {
    return(tibble(effect = "fixed", term = NA_character_,
                  estimate = NA_real_, std.error = NA_real_,
                  statistic = NA_real_, df = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
                  conf.low = NA_real_, conf.high = NA_real_,
                  status = res$status, note = res$note))
  }
  eligible <- res$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS
  broom.mixed::tidy(res$fit, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(
      p.value   = if (eligible) p.value   else NA_real_,
      conf.low  = if (eligible) conf.low  else NA_real_,
      conf.high = if (eligible) conf.high else NA_real_,
      status    = res$status,
      note      = res$note
    )
}
```

## 1.4 The run record: what this run reads, and clearing what it will write

```{r run-record}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every file this notebook writes is tied to one run of it.
#
#   RUN_START     the clock time at which this run began. The manifest at
#                 the end of section 11 compares each output's modification
#                 time against it, so a file this run did not write reads as
#                 not written this run.
#   INPUT_SHA256  the SHA-256 checksum of each input file, a 64-character
#                 fingerprint of the file's exact bytes that changes if any
#                 byte of the file changes.
#   RUN_ID        the start time followed by the first eight characters of a
#                 checksum taken over the input checksums, so two runs on the
#                 same inputs share the suffix and a run on different inputs
#                 does not. Study1_01_Quant.Rmd builds its run identifier the
#                 same way.
#
# The previous run's manifest is deleted here, before anything else is
# written, so a run that stops part way leaves no manifest, and a file
# downstream that requires one cannot take a half-finished set of outputs
# for a finished one.
#
# clear_outputs() is called at the top of every chunk that writes a file. It
# deletes that chunk's outputs from the previous run before the chunk
# computes anything, so a chunk that fails leaves its files missing rather
# than leaving the previous run's copies in place, and it adds each path to
# INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS, the list the manifest is built from. The one file in
# this folder tree that is kept from run to run on purpose is the
# matched-removal cache of section 5.5, which checks its own key.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
RUN_START <- Sys.time()

INPUT_FILES <- c(
  long_data         = PATH_LONG,
  text_measures     = PATH_MEASURES,
  text_wordcounts   = PATH_WORDCOUNTS,
  text_vocabulary   = PATH_VOCAB,
  text_tokens       = PATH_TOKENS,
  text_affect       = PATH_AFFECT,
  text_topics       = PATH_TOPICS,
  topics_top_words  = PATH_TOPIC_WORDS
)
stopifnot(all(file.exists(INPUT_FILES)))
INPUT_SHA256 <- unname(tools::sha256sum(INPUT_FILES))

# tools::sha256sum() reads files, so the checksum over the input checksums is
# taken on a temporary file holding them one per line.
input_hash_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
writeLines(INPUT_SHA256, input_hash_file)
RUN_ID <- paste0(format(RUN_START, "%Y%m%dT%H%M%S"), "-",
                 substr(unname(tools::sha256sum(input_hash_file)), 1, 8))
unlink(input_hash_file)

PATH_RUN_MANIFEST <- file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                               "study1_integration_run_manifest.csv")
unlink(PATH_RUN_MANIFEST)

INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS <- character(0)
clear_outputs <- function(...) {
  paths <- c(...)
  INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS <<- union(INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS, paths)
  unlink(paths)
  invisible(paths)
}

run_inputs <- tibble(
  run_id = RUN_ID,
  input  = names(INPUT_FILES),
  file   = basename(INPUT_FILES),
  bytes  = unname(file.size(INPUT_FILES)),
  sha256 = INPUT_SHA256
)
cat("RUN_ID =", RUN_ID, "\n")
print(as.data.frame(run_inputs %>% select(input, file, bytes, sha256)))
```

# 2. Load and join

## 2.1 Why the ratings and the flags live in two different files

```{r join-rationale, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("
The measurement step must never be able to see which experimental arm a
response came from. If the person or the program writing the search patterns
can see the condition, the patterns can drift, even without anyone intending
it, toward whatever produces the expected difference. Every count in this
notebook would then be unfalsifiable.

So the two halves of the analysis are kept in separate files with separate
columns. `study1_long_with_text.csv` holds the condition (`Type`) and the
`rating`, and is read only here. `nlp/study1_text_measures.csv` holds the
flags and has no condition column and no rating column; the notebook that
writes it checks this before saving. The blind, the separation of the
measures from the condition, is therefore enforced by the files themselves,
not by anyone's discipline, and the check in section 2.3 repeats it from
this side. The word, token, affect and topic tables that sections 8 and 9
read are held to the same rule and checked the same way.
")
```

## 2.2 Read both files

```{r load-inputs, message=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read the ratings file, keeping only the five columns this notebook needs:
# the three columns that together name a response (id, stimulus_id,
# dimension), the experimental arm (Type) and the rating. Demographics and
# the raw text are not read. Nothing here analyses them, and reading them
# would only invite someone to.
#
# col_types is given explicitly rather than left for readr to guess. `id` is
# read as character because it is a subject-pool identifier, not a quantity;
# read as a number it could lose a leading zero or be compared with `<`.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ratings <- read_csv(
  PATH_LONG,
  col_types = cols_only(
    id          = col_character(),
    Type        = col_character(),
    stimulus_id = col_character(),
    dimension   = col_character(),
    rating      = col_double()
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Type      = factor(Type,      levels = TYPE_LEVELS),
    dimension = factor(dimension, levels = DIM_LEVELS)
  )

cat("Ratings file:", nrow(ratings), "rows,",
    n_distinct(ratings$id), "participants.\n")
print(ratings %>% distinct(id, Type) %>% count(Type, name = "n_participants"))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Read the flags file. Every column is named here, because the file has a
# contract, a fixed list of the columns the notebook writes, and a missing or
# extra column is an error to catch at once rather than three sections
# later.
#
# The read is a function rather than a bare call so that the column list, the
# column types and the factor conversions live in one place, beside the
# contract check in section 2.3 that names the same columns.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
read_flags_file <- function(path) {
  read_csv(
    path,
    col_types = cols(
      id             = col_character(),
      stimulus_id    = col_character(),
      stimulus_num   = col_integer(),
      stimulus_type  = col_character(),
      dimension      = col_character(),
      n_words        = col_integer(),
      says_detail    = col_logical(),
      says_time      = col_logical(),
      says_skill     = col_logical(),
      # says_concept marks a justification that talks about the idea, meaning,
      # thought, message or story behind the work rather than about its surface.
      # It is the creativity-side counterpart of says_detail, says_time and
      # says_skill, and it is what makes section 4 possible.
      says_concept   = col_logical(),
      says_prompt    = col_logical(),
      # says_machine_made is the narrow companion of says_prompt. Where
      # says_prompt fires on any machine, prompting or generating word,
      # says_machine_made fires only when the response mentions a machine
      # MAKING the work: a machine noun followed closely by a making verb
      # ("the AI generated this"), a making verb followed by "by", "with",
      # "using" or "from" and a machine noun ("made with an AI"), or a
      # compound such as "ai-generated". A sentence in which a person is the
      # agent of tool use ("Alex used a program") does not fire it. The flag
      # records the mention whichever way it points, so "this does not look
      # AI generated" fires it too.
      says_machine_made = col_logical(),
      # machine_made_reading says which way those mentions pointed: asserted,
      # not_asserted (every matched phrase negated or conditional), or neither
      # (exactly when says_machine_made is FALSE). The "asserted" set is the
      # narrow count of section 5.
      machine_made_reading = col_character(),
      prior_exposure = col_character(),
      # anchor_echo is TRUE when a response contains the rating scale's own
      # wording ("a great deal of effort involved"). It records that the
      # wording is present, not that the response says nothing else.
      anchor_echo    = col_logical(),
      # The four polarity columns say which way a flagged mention pointed. Each
      # topic flag records a TOPIC and not an endorsement: "barely any detail"
      # is detail talk, because detail is what the writer is discussing. The
      # polarity column beside a flag records whether the first matched phrase
      # sat inside a negation ("not much detail", "no real skill", "did not
      # take much time"), in which case it is "negated"; "asserted" otherwise;
      # and "neither" exactly when the flag itself is FALSE. The reading looks
      # a short way back from the first match and no further, so it is a rough
      # guide to direction rather than a parse of the sentence. They are read
      # as character here and turned into factors below. They are description
      # only (sections 3.1.2, 3.2, 4.1.2 and 4.2), and no registered test
      # reads them.
      detail_polarity  = col_character(),
      time_polarity    = col_character(),
      skill_polarity   = col_character(),
      concept_polarity = col_character()
    )
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      dimension      = factor(dimension,      levels = DIM_LEVELS),
      stimulus_type  = factor(stimulus_type,  levels = STIMTYPE_LEVELS),
      prior_exposure = factor(prior_exposure, levels = EXPOSURE_LEVELS),
      machine_made_reading = factor(machine_made_reading,
                                    levels = MACHINE_READING_LEVELS),
      across(ends_with("_polarity"), ~ factor(.x, levels = POLARITY_LEVELS))
    )
}

measures <- read_flags_file(PATH_MEASURES)

cat("Flags file:", nrow(measures), "rows,",
    n_distinct(measures$id), "participants.\n")
```

## 2.3 Check the contract, then join

```{r join-and-assert}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE CONTRACT. The flags file must have exactly these nineteen columns, in
# this set, and must not contain the condition, the rating or the text. We
# check both directions: nothing missing, nothing extra.
#
# How the nineteen break down. Five columns name the response (the
# participant, the image, its number, its kind, and the rating dimension the
# justification was written for); one is the word count; five are the yes/no
# topic flags (detail, time, skill, concept, prompting); one is the yes/no
# machine-authorship flag, says_machine_made, which fires when the response
# mentions a machine making the work; one, machine_made_reading, says
# whether that mention was asserted; one is the three-way prior-exposure
# category; one is the anchor-echo flag, which marks a response containing
# the rating scale's own wording; and the last four are the polarity
# columns, one for each of the detail, time, skill and concept flags, each
# taking asserted, negated or neither. If the check below reports
# machine_made_reading or the polarity columns missing, Study1_02_Text.ipynb
# has not been run with those steps; run it and the file will match.
#
# The check is a function that takes the file's label, so that the contract
# is stated once and every message it raises names the file it is about.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CONTRACT_COLS <- c(
  "id", "stimulus_id", "stimulus_num", "stimulus_type", "dimension",
  "n_words", "says_detail", "says_time", "says_skill", "says_concept",
  "says_prompt", "says_machine_made", "machine_made_reading",
  "prior_exposure", "anchor_echo",
  "detail_polarity", "time_polarity", "skill_polarity", "concept_polarity"
)

# The columns no file from the measurement step may carry. Sections 8 and 9
# check their tables against the same list.
FORBIDDEN_COLS <- c("Type", "rating", "response_text", "condition")

check_flags_contract <- function(m, label = "The text-measures file") {
  # The blind check comes first, so that a broken blind is reported as one
  # rather than as an extra column.
  present <- intersect(FORBIDDEN_COLS, names(m))
  if (length(present) > 0) {
    stop("BLIND BROKEN: ", label, " contains ",
         paste(present, collapse = ", "),
         ". Every count in this notebook is suspect. Fix Study1_02_Text.ipynb.")
  }

  missing_cols <- setdiff(CONTRACT_COLS, names(m))
  extra_cols   <- setdiff(names(m), CONTRACT_COLS)

  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(label, " is missing required columns: ",
         paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (length(extra_cols) > 0) {
    stop(label, " has columns it should not have: ",
         paste(extra_cols, collapse = ", "))
  }

  # machine_made_reading is tied to its flag in the same way the polarity
  # columns are tied to theirs: "neither" exactly when says_machine_made is
  # FALSE.
  mm_reading <- as.character(m$machine_made_reading)
  if (anyNA(mm_reading)) {
    stop(label, ": machine_made_reading has values outside ",
         "asserted / not_asserted / neither.")
  }
  n_untied_mm <- sum((mm_reading == "neither") != !m$says_machine_made)
  if (n_untied_mm > 0) {
    stop(label, ": machine_made_reading and says_machine_made disagree on ",
         n_untied_mm, " row(s).")
  }

  # The polarity columns are tied to their flags: "neither" exactly when the
  # flag is FALSE, and asserted or negated exactly when it is TRUE. A row that
  # breaks that tie means the notebook computed the polarity from a different
  # match than the one it recorded as the flag, and nothing built on the pair
  # is safe. A value outside the three agreed categories arrives here as NA,
  # because the factor conversion in read_flags_file() has no level for it.
  for (topic in c("detail", "time", "skill", "concept")) {
    flag <- m[[paste0("says_", topic)]]
    pol  <- as.character(m[[paste0(topic, "_polarity")]])
    if (anyNA(pol)) {
      stop(label, ": ", topic, "_polarity has values outside ",
           "asserted / negated / neither.")
    }
    n_untied <- sum((pol == "neither") != !flag)
    if (n_untied > 0) {
      stop(label, ": ", topic, "_polarity and says_", topic, " disagree on ",
           n_untied, " row(s). 'neither' must appear exactly where the flag ",
           "is FALSE.")
    }
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

check_flags_contract(measures)
cat("Contract check passed: the flags file has the ", length(CONTRACT_COLS),
    " agreed columns, neither the condition nor the rating, and polarity ",
    "and reading columns that agree with their flags.\n", sep = "")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The join key is (id, stimulus_id, dimension), the three columns that
# together name one response. `relationship = "one-to-one"` makes dplyr stop
# if either side has a duplicated key. A duplicated key turns a join into a
# partial cross product, every pairing of the duplicated rows, and inflates n
# without any visible sign.
#
# `na_matches = "never"` stops rows with a missing key from matching each
# other, which is the other way a join can create rows that do not exist.
#
# The flags file has a row for every response the ratings file has,
# including any response with no usable text, whose flags are simply FALSE.
# The two files must therefore name exactly the same set of responses, and
# the run stops at assertion (b) below if either carries a response the
# other lacks. A truncated flags file would otherwise shrink every model in
# this notebook without anything visibly going wrong.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_join_check.csv"))

n_ratings_before  <- nrow(ratings)
n_measures_before <- nrow(measures)

dat <- run_or_report("join ratings to flags", function() {
  inner_join(
    ratings, measures,
    by           = c("id", "stimulus_id", "dimension"),
    relationship = "one-to-one",
    na_matches   = "never"
  )
})
stopifnot(!is.null(dat))

# Post-join assertions. Each one states an expectation in words first.
# (a) The join must not have invented rows: the result can be no larger than
#     the smaller input.
stopifnot(nrow(dat) <= min(n_ratings_before, n_measures_before))
# (b) Every flagged response must have found its rating, and every rating its
#     flags. If either fails, the two files disagree about the response key
#     and nothing downstream is trustworthy.
if (nrow(dat) != n_measures_before) {
  stop("Join lost ", n_measures_before - nrow(dat), " flagged responses. ",
       "The two files disagree on (id, stimulus_id, dimension).")
}
if (nrow(dat) != n_ratings_before) {
  stop("Join lost ", n_ratings_before - nrow(dat), " rated responses that ",
       "have no row in the flags file. The two files disagree on ",
       "(id, stimulus_id, dimension).")
}
# (c) The key must still uniquely identify a row.
stopifnot(nrow(distinct(dat, id, stimulus_id, dimension)) == nrow(dat))
# (d) Every participant kept their arm, and nobody appears in two arms.
stopifnot(nrow(distinct(dat, id, Type)) == n_distinct(dat$id))

# The narrow set of section 5 as a true/false column: the response states
# that the work is or looks machine-made.
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(states_machine_made = machine_made_reading == "asserted")

join_check <- tibble(
  quantity = c("rows in ratings file", "rows in flags file",
               "rows after join", "responses with text but no rating match",
               "ratings with no text (dropped)",
               "participants", "participants in Human arm",
               "participants in AI arm"),
  value    = c(n_ratings_before, n_measures_before, nrow(dat),
               n_measures_before - nrow(dat),
               n_ratings_before - nrow(dat),
               n_distinct(dat$id),
               n_distinct(dat$id[dat$Type == "Human"]),
               n_distinct(dat$id[dat$Type == "AI"]))
)
join_check
write_csv(join_check, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_join_check.csv"))
```

## 2.4 What the corpus looks like

```{r corpus-check}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One table to read before any statistics: how long the justifications are
# and how often each flag fires overall. It is not a result but the
# denominator behind every result. A flag that fires in 0.5% or 95% of
# responses cannot support an inference either way, so the rates are worth
# seeing before the models.
#
# `anchor_echo` is included as orientation rather than as a finding: it marks
# responses that contain the rating scale's own wording ("a great deal of
# effort involved"). It cannot tell an answer that only hands the wording
# back from one that goes on to give a reason ("a great deal of effort,
# because every edge was painted by hand"), so its rate says how often the
# scale's words were borrowed, not how many answers said nothing else.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_text_corpus_check.csv",
                                        "study1_text_corpus_by_dimension.csv")))

corpus_check <- dat %>%
  summarise(
    n_responses      = n(),
    n_participants   = n_distinct(id),
    words_median     = median(n_words, na.rm = TRUE),
    words_mean       = mean(n_words,   na.rm = TRUE),
    words_p10        = quantile(n_words, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    words_p90        = quantile(n_words, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    rate_detail      = mean(says_detail),
    rate_time        = mean(says_time),
    rate_skill       = mean(says_skill),
    rate_concept     = mean(says_concept),
    rate_prompt      = mean(says_prompt),
    rate_machine_made = mean(says_machine_made),
    rate_machine_made_asserted = mean(states_machine_made),
    rate_exposure_asserted = mean(prior_exposure == "asserted"),
    rate_exposure_negated  = mean(prior_exposure == "negated"),
    rate_anchor_echo = mean(anchor_echo)
  )
glimpse(corpus_check)
write_csv(corpus_check, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_corpus_check.csv"))

# The same table split by dimension. The flags are expected to behave very
# differently in effort and in creativity justifications, and the split shows
# that before section 3 builds on it.
corpus_by_dim <- dat %>%
  group_by(dimension) %>%
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    words_median = median(n_words, na.rm = TRUE),
    rate_detail  = mean(says_detail),
    rate_time    = mean(says_time),
    rate_skill   = mean(says_skill),
    rate_concept = mean(says_concept),
    rate_prompt  = mean(says_prompt),
    rate_machine_made = mean(says_machine_made),
    rate_machine_made_asserted = mean(states_machine_made),
    rate_asserted = mean(prior_exposure == "asserted"),
    rate_anchor  = mean(anchor_echo),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
corpus_by_dim
write_csv(corpus_by_dim,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_corpus_by_dimension.csv"))
```

## 2.5 The resampling helper used by every interval in this file

```{r bootstrap-helper}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT "RESAMPLING PARTICIPANTS" MEANS, AND WHY IT IS THE RIGHT UNIT.
#
# A confidence interval answers a question: if this study were run again with
# a new sample from the same population, how much would this number move? The
# bootstrap answers it by simulation. It builds many pretend re-runs out of
# the data already collected, recomputes the number in each, and reads the
# middle 95% of the resulting spread.
#
# The choice that matters is what gets resampled. The 2,220 responses are not
# 2,220 independent observations: they come from 111 people, each of whom
# contributed 20. People differ systematically in how effusive they are, how
# often they mention detail, how high they rate. If we resampled RESPONSES,
# the pretend re-runs would each contain a fresh mix of one person's responses
# with another's, which understates how much a number moves when whole people
# are swapped out. Swapping out whole people is what running the study again
# would do, so the interval would come out far too narrow.
#
# So the bootstrap resamples participants: it draws 111 participant
# identifiers with replacement, takes all 20 responses from each drawn person,
# and recomputes.
# A person drawn twice contributes their whole block twice. This preserves
# the within-person structure and puts the sampling variability at the level
# where it lives.
#
# The interval is a "percentile interval": the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of
# the 2,000 recomputed values. It makes no assumption that the statistic is
# normally distributed, which matters here because most of our statistics are
# proportions near the edges of their range.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

boot_by_participant <- function(df, stat_fun, B = B_BOOT, seed = 20260421L) {
  # Pre-compute, once, which rows belong to which participant. Rebuilding the
  # resampled data frame is then a single index lookup instead of a filter,
  # which is what makes 2,000 replications finish in seconds.
  idx_by_id <- split(seq_len(nrow(df)), as.character(df$id))
  ids       <- names(idx_by_id)
  n_ids     <- length(ids)

  observed <- stat_fun(df)
  k        <- length(observed)

  set.seed(seed)
  reps <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = k)
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    drawn <- sample(ids, n_ids, replace = TRUE)
    rows  <- unlist(idx_by_id[drawn], use.names = FALSE)
    val   <- stat_fun(df[rows, , drop = FALSE])
    # A replicate can be undefined, for example when no drawn participant used
    # the "negated" category, so that its mean rating has no value. Such a
    # replicate is recorded as NA rather than stopping the run, and n_valid
    # reports how many replicates were defined, so the reader can judge
    # whether the interval is stable.
    if (length(val) == k) reps[b, ] <- val
  }

  ci_lo <- apply(reps, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  ci_hi <- apply(reps, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)

  tibble(
    quantity   = if (!is.null(names(observed))) names(observed)
                 else paste0("q", seq_len(k)),
    estimate   = as.numeric(observed),
    ci_lo      = ci_lo,
    ci_hi      = ci_hi,
    B          = B,
    n_valid    = apply(reps, 2, function(x) sum(!is.na(x))),
    resampled  = "participants, with replacement"
  )
}
```

# 3. What people meant by "effort"

```{r effort-scope}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Everything in this section is restricted to (a) the human-attribution arm
# and (b) effort justifications.
#
# Why the human arm only: the question is what "effort" means when the work is
# believed to be human-made, because that is the belief the sweat-of-the-brow
# doctrine was written about. In the AI arm, effort talk is partly talk about
# what a machine does, which is a different construct (a different thing for
# the measure to capture) under the same word. The AI arm is not discarded; it
# is the subject of section 6. It does not belong in this section's
# denominators.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
effort_human <- dat %>%
  filter(Type == "Human", dimension == "effort") %>%
  # Word count, standardised (mean 0, SD 1) so that when it enters a model as
  # a control in section 3.2 its coefficient reads as "rating points per one
  # standard deviation of extra writing" and the other coefficients keep their
  # ordinary meaning at an average-length response.
  mutate(n_words_z = as.numeric(scale(n_words)))

cat("Effort justifications in the human-attribution arm: ",
    nrow(effort_human), " responses from ",
    n_distinct(effort_human$id), " participants.\n", sep = "")
```

## 3.1 How often each kind of effort talk appears

```{r effort-prevalence}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three competing readings of "effort", each with its own search pattern:
#
#   detail talk:  visible detail, intricacy, complexity, texture, shading,
#                 brushwork, or sheer quantity of content ("a lot going on").
#                 This is effort inferred from the artifact.
#   time talk:    hours, duration, tediousness, "took forever".
#                 This is effort as industriousness, and it is the reading the
#                 sweat-of-the-brow doctrine assumes.
#   skill talk:   skill, craft, technique, talent, training, mastery.
#                 This is not sweat-of-the-brow at all; it is closer to the
#                 creativity dimension, and copyright treats it differently.
#
# The three are not mutually exclusive: one sentence can mention detail and
# time. The percentages therefore need not sum to 100%. The table also
# reports how often a response mentions none of the three, the share of
# responses about whose meaning these rules say nothing.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_prevalence.csv"))

effort_rates_fun <- function(d) {
  c(
    detail = mean(d$says_detail),
    time   = mean(d$says_time),
    skill  = mean(d$says_skill),
    none_of_the_three = mean(!d$says_detail & !d$says_time & !d$says_skill)
  )
}

effort_prevalence <- run_or_report(
  "3.1 effort-talk prevalence with participant-resampled CI",
  function() {
    boot_by_participant(effort_human, effort_rates_fun) %>%
      mutate(
        arm       = "Human",
        dimension = "effort",
        n_responses    = nrow(effort_human),
        n_participants = n_distinct(effort_human$id)
      ) %>%
      relocate(arm, dimension)
  }
)

if (!is.null(effort_prevalence)) {
  effort_prevalence %>%
    mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi), ~ pct(.x))) %>%
    print()
  write_csv(effort_prevalence,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_prevalence.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the ordering of the three estimates. The intervals describe
# how far each rate would move under a fresh sample of participants; they do
# not decide whether two rates differ, and reading them that way is the error
# the registered comparison exists to prevent (two intervals can overlap while
# the difference between the rates is reliably non-zero, because both rates
# come from the same participants and move together). The comparison is the
# model in 3.1.1 below. If detail talk comes out ahead of time talk there,
# the effort rating is reading the picture, not the process. That is the
# opposite of what the sweat-of-the-brow mapping assumes, and the paper should
# say so plainly.
```

### 3.1.1 The registered comparisons: detail against time, detail against skill

```{r text-test-helpers}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE REGISTERED COMPARISON IS ONE MODEL, NOT TWO RATES SET SIDE BY SIDE.
#
# The preregistration names five directional tests over the written
# explanations and gives four of them the same shape. For a given arm and a
# given rating dimension, the two flags being compared are stacked: every
# response contributes two rows, one saying whether it mentioned the first
# topic and one saying whether it mentioned the second. The stacked yes/no
# outcome is modelled as a mixed logistic regression:
#
#   flag ~ measure + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),   family = binomial
#
# "Logistic" means the model works on the log-odds of a mention, the
# logarithm of the probability of a mention divided by the probability of no
# mention. On that scale a true-or-false outcome can be modelled with a
# straight line. "Mixed" means it carries random intercepts: every
# participant gets their own baseline rate of mentioning things at all, and
# every image gets its own, so that the twenty stacked rows from one talkative
# person are not counted as twenty independent votes. Counting them that way
# would make every standard error here far too small.
#
# The one coefficient that matters is the `measure` term: the log-odds of
# mentioning the first topic minus the log-odds of mentioning the second, for
# the same person looking at the same image. A positive value says the first
# topic was the more common one. Each comparison names in advance which topic
# is predicted to come out ahead, and the table records whether it did.
#
# Two things are recorded that a bare coefficient would hide. First, the
# fit's status from fit_mixed() in section 1.3: whether the optimiser
# reported any trouble converging, and whether the fit is singular, meaning
# one of the two random-intercept variances was driven to exactly zero, which
# signals that the data cannot support that intercept. Both go into the
# `note` column beside the estimate, which opens with the status word, rather
# than scrolling past in the console. A fit whose status is not ok
# or singular keeps its estimate but carries no standard error, z or p-value.
# Second, a fit that fails outright is kept as a row with an empty estimate
# and the failure message, so the family in section 7 still has its five
# members and the correction is applied over five rather than over however
# many happened to run.
#
# The four pair comparisons are written down once, in the list below, and
# every place that runs one of them reads it from there: 3.1.1 runs the two
# effort pairs and 4.1.1 the two creativity pairs. A single copy of the
# specification is what makes "the same model for all four" a fact about the
# code rather than a promise.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

TEXT_PAIR_TESTS <- list(
  detail_vs_time = list(
    comparison = "detail vs time",  arm = "Human", dimension = "effort",
    flag_a = "says_detail",  name_a = "detail",
    flag_b = "says_time",    name_b = "time",
    predicted = "detail > time"
  ),
  detail_vs_skill = list(
    comparison = "detail vs skill", arm = "Human", dimension = "effort",
    flag_a = "says_detail",  name_a = "detail",
    flag_b = "says_skill",   name_b = "skill",
    predicted = "detail > skill"
  ),
  concept_vs_execution = list(
    comparison = "concept vs execution", arm = "Human", dimension = "creativity",
    flag_a = "says_concept", name_a = "concept",
    # Execution talk is the visible-detail flag read inside creativity
    # justifications, exactly as in section 4.1.
    flag_b = "says_detail",  name_b = "execution",
    predicted = "concept > execution"
  ),
  concept_vs_novelty = list(
    comparison = "concept vs novelty", arm = "Human", dimension = "creativity",
    flag_a = "says_concept", name_a = "concept",
    # Novelty talk is the three-way prior-exposure category collapsed to
    # "raised at all, in either direction", the same quantity section 4.1
    # reports as novelty_either. The column is built inside fit_pair_test().
    flag_b = "novelty_raised", name_b = "novelty",
    predicted = "concept > novelty"
  )
)

# Each mixed logistic regression is fitted by fit_mixed() from section 1.3,
# with family = binomial. That helper restarts a fit whose first pass stopped
# short, records what the optimiser and lme4 said, and gives the fit its
# status. A fit that stopped on a slope can carry standard errors that are
# implausibly small or large. Standard errors are computed from the curvature
# at the stopping point, and that point is not the top of the likelihood, so
# such a fit carries no p-value below.

# Read one coefficient off a fitted model as a one-row table, or return the
# same row with empty numbers when the fit does not exist. The z statistic is
# the estimate divided by its standard error. The p-value is from the
# two-sided Wald test, which summary() reports for a logistic mixed model. The
# test asks how many standard errors the estimate sits from zero, and how
# often a gap at least that large would arise by chance if the true value
# were zero. A fit whose status does not permit inference keeps its estimate
# and loses the other three numbers.
coef_row <- function(res, term) {
  if (is.null(res$fit)) {
    return(tibble(term = term, estimate_log_odds = NA_real_, se = NA_real_,
                  z = NA_real_, p_raw = NA_real_, status = res$status))
  }
  co <- summary(res$fit)$coefficients
  stopifnot(term %in% rownames(co))
  eligible <- res$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS
  tibble(
    term              = term,
    estimate_log_odds = unname(co[term, "Estimate"]),
    se                = if (eligible) unname(co[term, "Std. Error"]) else NA_real_,
    z                 = if (eligible) unname(co[term, "z value"]) else NA_real_,
    p_raw             = if (eligible) unname(co[term, "Pr(>|z|)"]) else NA_real_,
    status            = res$status
  )
}

# Turn a signed estimate into the words the preregistration uses, so that the
# predicted and observed directions can be compared as strings.
direction_words <- function(estimate, name_a, name_b) {
  if (is.na(estimate)) return(NA_character_)
  if (estimate > 0) paste(name_a, ">", name_b)
  else if (estimate < 0) paste(name_a, "<", name_b)
  else paste(name_a, "=", name_b)
}

# One registered pair comparison, from the specification to the table row.
# `dat_x` is the joined ratings-plus-flags frame; the function does its own
# filtering to the arm and dimension the specification names, so the caller
# cannot accidentally hand it the wrong subset.
fit_pair_test <- function(spec, dat_x) {
  d <- dat_x %>%
    filter(Type == spec$arm, dimension == spec$dimension) %>%
    mutate(novelty_raised = prior_exposure != "neither")

  # Stack the two flags. Each response becomes two rows, one per measure.
  # `measure` is a factor whose reference level is the SECOND topic, so that
  # the single coefficient reads as "first topic minus second topic" and a
  # positive value is the predicted direction.
  long <- bind_rows(
    d %>% transmute(id, stimulus_id, measure = spec$name_a,
                    flag = as.integer(.data[[spec$flag_a]])),
    d %>% transmute(id, stimulus_id, measure = spec$name_b,
                    flag = as.integer(.data[[spec$flag_b]]))
  ) %>%
    mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = c(spec$name_b, spec$name_a)))

  res <- fit_mixed(
    flag ~ measure + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), long, family = binomial,
    step = paste("registered text test:", spec$comparison)
  )
  row <- coef_row(res, paste0("measure", spec$name_a)) %>%
    mutate(
      comparison          = spec$comparison,
      arm                 = spec$arm,
      dimension           = spec$dimension,
      n_responses         = nrow(d),
      n_participants      = n_distinct(d$id),
      n_rows_stacked      = nrow(long),
      rate_a              = mean(d[[spec$flag_a]]),
      rate_b              = mean(d[[spec$flag_b]]),
      predicted_direction = spec$predicted,
      observed_direction  = direction_words(estimate_log_odds,
                                            spec$name_a, spec$name_b),
      direction_as_predicted = !is.na(observed_direction) &
                               observed_direction == predicted_direction,
      model = "flag ~ measure + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), binomial, bobyqa",
      note  = res$note
    ) %>%
    relocate(comparison, arm, dimension, n_responses, n_participants)

  # The stacked frame is returned with the fit so that the sensitivity check
  # in section 7.2 refits exactly the rows the registered model saw.
  list(row = row, fit = res$fit, stacked = long)
}
```

```{r effort-denotation-tests}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two effort comparisons, fitted within human-arm effort justifications.
# Both predict that visible detail comes out ahead: of time, which is the
# reading the sweat-of-the-brow doctrine assumes, and of skill, which is not
# labour at all. The uncorrected p-values are printed here; the corrected
# ones, and the verdict, wait for section 7, where the five tests are
# corrected together. A test read against .05 on its own p-value before the
# correction is applied is a test read twice.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
effort_pair_fits <- run_or_report(
  "3.1.1 detail vs time and detail vs skill, mixed logistic regressions",
  function() {
    lapply(TEXT_PAIR_TESTS[c("detail_vs_time", "detail_vs_skill")],
           fit_pair_test, dat_x = dat)
  }
)

denotation_effort_tests <- NULL
if (!is.null(effort_pair_fits)) {
  denotation_effort_tests <- bind_rows(lapply(effort_pair_fits, `[[`, "row"))
  denotation_effort_tests %>%
    select(comparison, n_responses, n_participants, rate_a, rate_b,
           estimate_log_odds, se, z, p_raw, predicted_direction,
           observed_direction, note) %>%
    print(width = Inf)
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the sign of estimate_log_odds (positive means detail talk
# was the more common of the two for the same person at the same image) and
# the note column. Do not read p_raw against .05 here; section 7 does that
# after the correction.
```

### 3.1.2 Asserted or denied: which way the flagged talk pointed

```{r effort-polarity-shares}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every topic flag records a topic and not an endorsement, so "incredibly
# detailed" and "barely any detail" are both detail talk. That is the right
# rule for the denotation question, since both writers say that detail is
# what effort meant to them. A reader will still want to know how often the
# flagged talk affirmed the topic and how often it denied it, and the polarity
# columns record that. Among the responses a flag fired on, this table
# gives the share whose matched phrase sat inside a negation ("not much
# detail", "no real skill", "did not take much time") and the share that did
# not.
#
# This is description only. No test is run on it and no prediction was
# registered about it. As with every text measure in this file, the writing
# followed the rating, so a denial beside a low score says what the writer
# reached for after choosing the score, not what produced it. The
# interval is the same participant-resampled percentile interval every other
# rate in this file uses: participants are drawn with replacement, and the
# share among the drawn participants' flagged responses is recomputed each
# time. A flag that fires rarely has few flagged responses behind it, and its
# interval is wide for that reason; a replicate in which no drawn participant
# tripped the flag has no defined share and is counted in n_valid.
#
# The helper runs on any arm-and-dimension subset, so 4.1.2 can apply it to
# creativity justifications without a second copy of the code.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

POLARITY_TOPICS <- c(detail  = "says_detail",  time    = "says_time",
                     skill   = "says_skill",   concept = "says_concept")

polarity_shares <- function(d, arm_label, dim_label) {
  bind_rows(lapply(names(POLARITY_TOPICS), function(topic) {
    flag_col  <- POLARITY_TOPICS[[topic]]
    pol_col   <- paste0(topic, "_polarity")
    share_fun <- function(dd) {
      pol <- as.character(dd[[pol_col]])[dd[[flag_col]]]
      c(share_asserted = mean(pol == "asserted"),
        share_negated  = mean(pol == "negated"))
    }
    boot_by_participant(d, share_fun) %>%
      mutate(
        topic      = topic,
        n_flagged  = sum(d[[flag_col]]),
        n_asserted = sum(d[[pol_col]] == "asserted"),
        n_negated  = sum(d[[pol_col]] == "negated"),
        .before = 1
      )
  })) %>%
    mutate(arm = arm_label, dimension = dim_label,
           n_responses = nrow(d), n_participants = n_distinct(d$id)) %>%
    relocate(arm, dimension)
}

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_polarity_shares.csv"))

effort_polarity <- run_or_report(
  "3.1.2 asserted vs negated shares among flagged effort justifications",
  function() polarity_shares(effort_human, "Human", "effort")
)

if (!is.null(effort_polarity)) {
  effort_polarity %>%
    select(topic, n_flagged, n_asserted, n_negated, quantity, estimate,
           ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>%
    mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi), ~ pct(.x))) %>%
    print(n = Inf)
  write_csv(effort_polarity,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_polarity_shares.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: share_negated for detail talk. If a noticeable share of the
# detail mentions in effort justifications were denials ("not much detail"),
# then detail is the vocabulary people reach for at BOTH ends of the effort
# scale, which says more about what the word denoted than a high rate of
# praise alone would.
```

## 3.2 Does detail talk go with a higher effort rating?

```{r effort-detail-lmm}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The prevalence above says what people talked about. This says whether the
# talk tracked the number they gave.
#
# The model: effort rating predicted by whether the justification mentioned
# visible detail, with random intercepts for participant and for image.
#
#   rating ~ says_detail + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# A "random intercept" for participant means the model gives each person their
# own baseline generosity, and the random intercept for image does the same
# for the ten pictures: some images simply draw higher effort ratings. What
# the participant intercept does not do is confine the detail coefficient to
# variation within a person. People who mention detail in many of their ten
# explanations may also rate higher overall, and the coefficient draws on
# that between-person difference as well as on the contrast between one
# person's detailed and plain explanations; it is a mixed-model association
# of the two together. Section 4.3.4 shows how to pull the two apart, for the
# familiarity measure, where the preregistration asks for the within-person
# part. Here the coefficient is description of what detail talk accompanied.
#
# This is the same random-effects structure Study1_01_Quant.Rmd uses for its
# primary models, deliberately: the two files should differ in what they ask,
# not in how they handle dependence.
#
# THE LENGTH OBJECTION. People who write more have more chances to trip any
# search pattern, and they may also rate differently. So the second model
# adds the response's word count as a covariate, a variable entered to hold
# length constant (standardised, so the intercept stays interpretable). If
# the detail coefficient survives, the association is not just an artifact of
# length.
#
# Each fit goes through fit_mixed() (section 1.3), so its status and note sit
# beside its coefficients and a fit that did not converge carries no p-value
# or interval.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_text_effort_detail_lmm.csv",
                                        "study1_text_effort_other_lmm.csv")))

effort_detail_res <- run_or_report(
  "3.2 effort ~ detail talk, mixed-effects model",
  function() {
    fit_mixed(rating ~ says_detail + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
              effort_human, step = "3.2 effort ~ detail talk")
  }
)
effort_detail_fit <- effort_detail_res$fit

effort_detail_res_len <- run_or_report(
  "3.2 effort ~ detail talk + word count, mixed-effects model",
  function() {
    fit_mixed(rating ~ says_detail + n_words_z + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
              effort_human, step = "3.2 effort ~ detail talk + word count")
  }
)

effort_detail_table <- run_or_report(
  "3.2 tidy both detail models",
  function() {
    bind_rows(
      tidy_mixed(effort_detail_res) %>%
        mutate(model = "rating ~ detail talk"),
      tidy_mixed(effort_detail_res_len) %>%
        mutate(model = "rating ~ detail talk + word count")
    ) %>%
      relocate(model) %>%
      mutate(
        arm       = "Human",
        dimension = "effort"
      )
  }
)

if (!is.null(effort_detail_table)) {
  print(effort_detail_table)
  write_csv(effort_detail_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_detail_lmm.csv"))
}

# The same model for time talk and for skill talk, so the three readings of
# "effort" are fitted on equal terms, not only the one that came out most
# common.
effort_other_table <- run_or_report(
  "3.2 effort ~ time talk and ~ skill talk, mixed-effects models",
  function() {
    fit_one <- function(flag) {
      f <- stats::as.formula(
        paste0("rating ~ ", flag, " + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)")
      )
      res <- fit_mixed(f, effort_human,
                       step = paste0("3.2 effort ~ ", flag))
      tidy_mixed(res) %>%
        mutate(model = paste0("rating ~ ", flag))
    }
    bind_rows(fit_one("says_time"), fit_one("says_skill")) %>%
      relocate(model) %>%
      mutate(arm = "Human", dimension = "effort")
  }
)

if (!is.null(effort_other_table)) {
  print(effort_other_table)
  write_csv(effort_other_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_other_lmm.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the `estimate` for says_detailTRUE in the first model, in
# rating points on the 1-5 scale, and whether its confidence interval excludes
# zero. Then check that the estimate barely moves when word count enters, and
# that the status column reads ok or singular.
```

```{r effort-polarity-lmm}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The models above ask whether a response that raised a topic went with a
# different rating from one that did not. This splits the "raised it" side by
# polarity, so the flag becomes a three-level factor:
#
#   neither:   the topic was not raised (the reference level)
#   asserted:  it was raised and affirmed ("so much detail")
#   negated:   it was raised and denied ("not much detail")
#
#   rating ~ polarity + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# with the same random intercepts for participant and image as every model in
# this section, so each coefficient is a difference in rating points from a
# response that did not raise the topic, with each person's and each image's
# baseline allowed for; like the models above, it mixes the contrast within a
# person with differences between people who raise the topic more or less
# often. The natural expectation is that "asserted" sits above the reference
# and "negated" below it; a topic whose two polarities did not separate would
# be one that was not what the rating was about.
#
# DESCRIPTION ONLY. These are the descriptive models above with one factor
# recoded, and they inherit the limit stated in section 4.4: the writing
# followed the rating, so this is what the word denoted for people who had
# already chosen a number, not what moved the number. Nothing here enters the
# registered family in section 7.
#
# A polarity level with no responses behind it is dropped before fitting
# rather than left in as an all-zero column, and the levels that were present
# are recorded beside the estimates so the reader can see which contrasts the
# data could support.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

fit_polarity_lmm <- function(d, topic, arm_label, dim_label) {
  pol_col <- paste0(topic, "_polarity")
  dd <- d %>%
    mutate(polarity = droplevels(relevel(
      factor(as.character(.data[[pol_col]]), levels = POLARITY_LEVELS),
      ref = "neither"
    )))
  res <- fit_mixed(
    rating ~ polarity + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), dd,
    step = paste0(dim_label, " ~ ", topic, " polarity, ", arm_label, " arm")
  )
  tidy_mixed(res) %>%
    mutate(
      model          = paste0("rating ~ ", topic, " polarity"),
      topic          = topic,
      arm            = arm_label,
      dimension      = dim_label,
      n_neither      = sum(dd$polarity == "neither"),
      n_asserted     = sum(dd$polarity == "asserted"),
      n_negated      = sum(dd$polarity == "negated"),
      levels_present = paste(levels(dd$polarity), collapse = ", "),
      singular       = res$status == "singular"
    ) %>%
    relocate(model, topic, arm, dimension)
}

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_polarity_lmm.csv"))

effort_polarity_table <- run_or_report(
  "3.2 effort ~ polarity of detail, time and skill talk, mixed-effects models",
  function() {
    bind_rows(lapply(c("detail", "time", "skill"), function(topic) {
      fit_polarity_lmm(effort_human, topic, "Human", "effort")
    }))
  }
)

if (!is.null(effort_polarity_table)) {
  effort_polarity_table %>%
    select(model, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value,
           n_asserted, n_negated, levels_present) %>%
    print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
  write_csv(effort_polarity_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_polarity_lmm.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: for each topic, the polarityasserted and polaritynegated
# estimates and whether they sit on opposite sides of zero. Read them as a
# description of what the two kinds of mention accompanied, not as a test.
```

## 3.3 Across the ten images, does detail talk track the effort rating?

```{r effort-image-correlation}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 3.2 asked the question response by response. This asks it across
# images, which is a different question; section 4.4 sets out what an answer
# to it can and cannot show.
#
# For each of the ten artworks, compute two numbers in the human arm:
#   (1) the proportion of effort justifications that mention visible detail;
#   (2) the average effort rating.
# Then correlate the two across the ten images.
#
# If images that provoke detail talk are also the images that get high effort
# ratings, then "effort" as measured by this instrument is largely a judgment
# about how much is visible in the picture: a property of the artifact, not of
# the labour behind it. That is a claim about the construct, and it is the
# claim the Feist mapping most needs to survive.
#
# The correlation is over ten points, which is very few, so the interval will
# be wide and should be reported as wide. The interval comes from resampling
# participants, not images: both per-image numbers are recomputed inside each
# replicate from the drawn participants, so the interval reflects the
# uncertainty that comes from having sampled these 56 people. It does not
# reflect uncertainty from having chosen these ten images. Ten images are too
# few to resample, and the paper should say so.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c(
  "study1_text_image_detail_effort.csv",
  "study1_text_effort_image_corr.csv",
  "study1_text_effort_image_corr_rank.csv"
)))

image_stats <- effort_human %>%
  group_by(stimulus_id, stimulus_type, stimulus_num) %>%
  summarise(
    n_responses      = n(),
    detail_rate      = mean(says_detail),
    mean_effort      = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(stimulus_type, stimulus_num)

image_stats
write_csv(image_stats,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_image_detail_effort.csv"))

image_corr <- run_or_report(
  "3.3 image-level correlation, detail-talk rate vs mean effort rating",
  function() {
    corr_fun <- function(d) {
      s <- d %>%
        group_by(stimulus_id) %>%
        summarise(detail_rate = mean(says_detail),
                  mean_effort = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
                  .groups = "drop")
      # A replicate is usable only if at least three images are present and
      # both quantities vary; otherwise the correlation is undefined.
      if (nrow(s) < 3 || sd(s$detail_rate) == 0 || sd(s$mean_effort) == 0) {
        return(NA_real_)
      }
      c(pearson_r = suppressWarnings(
        cor(s$detail_rate, s$mean_effort, method = "pearson")))
    }
    boot_by_participant(effort_human, corr_fun) %>%
      mutate(
        arm        = "Human",
        dimension  = "effort",
        n_images   = nrow(image_stats),
        note       = "10 images; interval reflects participant sampling only"
      )
  }
)

if (!is.null(image_corr)) {
  print(image_corr)
  write_csv(image_corr,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_image_corr.csv"))
}

# The rank correlation as well, because with ten points one unusual image can
# drag a Pearson correlation around, and Spearman's rank version is much less
# sensitive to that.
image_corr_spearman <- run_or_report(
  "3.3 image-level rank correlation (Spearman)",
  function() {
    ct <- suppressWarnings(
      cor.test(image_stats$detail_rate, image_stats$mean_effort,
               method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
    )
    tibble(
      quantity = "spearman_rho",
      estimate = unname(ct$estimate),
      p_value  = ct$p.value,
      n_images = nrow(image_stats)
    )
  }
)
if (!is.null(image_corr_spearman)) {
  print(image_corr_spearman)
  write_csv(image_corr_spearman,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_effort_image_corr_rank.csv"))
}
```
