# 4. What people meant by "creativity"

```{r creativity-scope}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This section is section 3 asked of the other rating, and it is built the same
# way: prevalence first, then models, then the across-image pattern.
#
# WHY THIS QUESTION MATTERS MORE THAN SECTION 3's.
#
# Feist v. Rural Telephone kept creativity and threw out labour. Creativity is
# therefore the criterion that decides protection, and whatever the word
# denoted for these raters is what the doctrinally decisive quantity was
# measured as. Section 3 asks what "effort" was about. Leaving "creativity"
# unexamined would mean the paper questions the criterion the Supreme Court
# discarded and takes the surviving one on trust.
#
# THREE CANDIDATE ANSWERS, parallel to the three in section 3:
#
#   concept talk:    the idea, meaning, thought, message or story behind the
#                    work: "what it represents", "the thought behind it",
#                    "symbolic", "a deeper meaning". Creativity located in
#                    conception.
#   novelty talk:    whether the work looks new or looks familiar. Creativity
#                    located in unprecedentedness. Already measured, by the
#                    three-way prior_exposure category; section 4.3 is that
#                    component and reuses it rather than building a second
#                    novelty measure.
#   execution talk:  visible detail and rendering. Creativity located in the
#                    making. Already measured, by says_detail, which is the
#                    same flag section 3 used for effort; applying it to
#                    creativity justifications is what makes it an execution
#                    measure here.
#
# Only concept talk needed a new search pattern. The other two are existing
# columns read in a new place, which is deliberate: a measure that is used for
# two questions cannot have been tuned to produce the answer to either.
#
# Same restriction as section 3, for the same reason: the human-attribution arm
# only, so that "creativity" means creativity attributed to a person, which is
# the belief Feist was written about. The novelty component in 4.3 is the one
# place the AI arm is read as well: the preregistration estimates the
# prior-exposure association within each condition separately, so 4.3 fits
# the human arm and the AI arm as two models and reports each on its own. A
# model that pools the two arms with the arm as a covariate is kept beside
# them as supplementary description. The AI label lowers creativity ratings
# on its own, and a reader will want to see whether the within-arm estimates
# and the pooled one agree.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
creativity_human <- dat %>%
  filter(Type == "Human", dimension == "creativity") %>%
  # Standardised word count (mean 0, SD 1), exactly as in section 3, so the
  # length control in 4.2 reads as "rating points per one standard deviation of
  # extra writing" and the other coefficients keep their ordinary meaning.
  mutate(n_words_z = as.numeric(scale(n_words)))

# Both arms, split by dimension. These two are what the novelty component in
# 4.3 runs on, and they are defined here so that every subset this section uses
# is visible in one place.
creativity_all <- dat %>% filter(dimension == "creativity")
effort_all     <- dat %>% filter(dimension == "effort")

cat("Creativity justifications in the human-attribution arm: ",
    nrow(creativity_human), " responses from ",
    n_distinct(creativity_human$id), " participants.\n", sep = "")
```

## 4.1 How often each kind of creativity talk appears

```{r creativity-prevalence}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The mirror of section 3.1. Three readings of "creativity", each with its own
# rule written in advance, measured in creativity justifications in the human
# arm.
#
# As in section 3.1, the categories are not mutually exclusive (one sentence
# can praise the idea and the rendering), so the percentages need not sum to
# 100%. Novelty is reported in three pieces because it is a three-way
# category rather than a yes/no flag:
#
#   novelty_asserted:  the response says the work looks familiar, seen before,
#                      derivative or generic
#   novelty_negated:   the response explicitly denies familiarity ("I've never
#                      seen anything like this"), which is a rater volunteering
#                      that novelty mattered to them, in the positive direction
#   novelty_either:    either of the above; this is the number to compare with
#                      concept talk and execution talk, because it is the share
#                      of responses in which novelty was raised at all,
#                      whichever way it pointed
#
# none_of_the_three is the share of creativity justifications in which the
# rater raised none of the three candidate meanings. About those responses
# the rules have nothing to say.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_creativity_prevalence.csv"))

creativity_rates_fun <- function(d) {
  c(
    concept          = mean(d$says_concept),
    novelty_asserted = mean(d$prior_exposure == "asserted"),
    novelty_negated  = mean(d$prior_exposure == "negated"),
    novelty_either   = mean(d$prior_exposure != "neither"),
    execution        = mean(d$says_detail),
    none_of_the_three = mean(
      !d$says_concept & d$prior_exposure == "neither" & !d$says_detail
    )
  )
}

creativity_prevalence <- run_or_report(
  "4.1 creativity-talk prevalence with participant-resampled CI",
  function() {
    boot_by_participant(creativity_human, creativity_rates_fun) %>%
      mutate(
        arm       = "Human",
        dimension = "creativity",
        n_responses    = nrow(creativity_human),
        n_participants = n_distinct(creativity_human$id)
      ) %>%
      relocate(arm, dimension)
  }
)

if (!is.null(creativity_prevalence)) {
  creativity_prevalence %>%
    mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi), ~ pct(.x))) %>%
    print()
  write_csv(creativity_prevalence,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_creativity_prevalence.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the ordering of concept, novelty_either and execution. As in
# section 3.1, the intervals describe each rate's sampling uncertainty and do
# not decide whether two rates differ. The registered comparisons, concept
# against execution and concept against novelty, are the models in 4.1.1
# below. If execution talk rivals or beats concept talk there, the creativity
# rating, like an effort rating led by detail talk, is reading the surface of
# the picture, and the two ratings are less separate in concept than the
# doctrinal mapping needs them to be. If novelty talk is common, section 4.3
# is where its consequences are measured.
```

### 4.1.1 The registered comparisons: concept against execution, concept against novelty

```{r creativity-denotation-tests}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two creativity comparisons, on the model set out in 3.1.1 and read from
# the same specification list. Fitted within human-arm creativity
# justifications. Both predict that concept talk comes out ahead: of
# execution, which is the visible-detail flag read in creativity
# justifications, and of novelty, which is the prior-exposure category
# collapsed to "raised at all, in either direction".
#
# Concept against execution is the comparison the doctrinal argument turns
# on. If concept comes out ahead, creativity was understood as a property of
# the idea and effort (section 3) as a property of the surface, which is the
# distinction Feist draws. If execution comes out ahead here as well as in
# section 3, the two ratings denoted the same feature of the picture for these
# raters.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
creativity_pair_fits <- run_or_report(
  "4.1.1 concept vs execution and concept vs novelty, mixed logistic regressions",
  function() {
    lapply(TEXT_PAIR_TESTS[c("concept_vs_execution", "concept_vs_novelty")],
           fit_pair_test, dat_x = dat)
  }
)

denotation_creativity_tests <- NULL
if (!is.null(creativity_pair_fits)) {
  denotation_creativity_tests <- bind_rows(
    lapply(creativity_pair_fits, `[[`, "row")
  )
  denotation_creativity_tests %>%
    select(comparison, n_responses, n_participants, rate_a, rate_b,
           estimate_log_odds, se, z, p_raw, predicted_direction,
           observed_direction, note) %>%
    print(width = Inf)
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: as in 3.1.1, the sign and the note. The corrected p-values
# and the verdict are in section 7.
```

## 4.2 Does concept talk go with a higher creativity rating?

```{r creativity-concept-lmm}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The mirror of section 3.2, with the same models and the same reasoning.
#
#   rating ~ says_concept + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# A "random intercept" for participant, written (1 | id), gives each person
# their own baseline generosity, and the random intercept for image does the
# same for the ten pictures: some images simply draw higher creativity
# ratings. As in 3.2, the participant intercept does not confine the concept
# coefficient to variation within a person: people who write about ideas
# often may also rate higher overall, and the coefficient draws on that
# difference between people as well as on the contrast inside one person's
# ten explanations. It is a mixed-model association of the two together.
#
# THE LENGTH OBJECTION, handled as in 3.2. People who write more have more
# chances to trip any search pattern, and they may also rate differently, so
# the second model adds the standardised word count. If the concept
# coefficient survives, the association is not an artifact of length.
#
# The limit on reading all of this is set out in section 4.4: these models say
# what the word denoted, not what caused the number.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(
  file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_text_creativity_concept_lmm.csv",
                            "study1_text_creativity_execution_lmm.csv")),
  file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_creativity_concept.rds")
)

creativity_concept_res <- run_or_report(
  "4.2 creativity ~ concept talk, mixed-effects model",
  function() {
    fit_mixed(rating ~ says_concept + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
              creativity_human, step = "4.2 creativity ~ concept talk")
  }
)
creativity_concept_fit <- creativity_concept_res$fit

creativity_concept_res_len <- run_or_report(
  "4.2 creativity ~ concept talk + word count, mixed-effects model",
  function() {
    fit_mixed(rating ~ says_concept + n_words_z + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
              creativity_human,
              step = "4.2 creativity ~ concept talk + word count")
  }
)

creativity_concept_table <- run_or_report(
  "4.2 tidy both concept models",
  function() {
    bind_rows(
      tidy_mixed(creativity_concept_res) %>%
        mutate(model = "rating ~ concept talk"),
      tidy_mixed(creativity_concept_res_len) %>%
        mutate(model = "rating ~ concept talk + word count")
    ) %>%
      relocate(model) %>%
      mutate(
        arm       = "Human",
        dimension = "creativity"
      )
  }
)

if (!is.null(creativity_concept_table)) {
  print(creativity_concept_table)
  write_csv(creativity_concept_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_creativity_concept_lmm.csv"))
}

# The execution component on the same terms. This is says_detail, the
# section 3 flag, read inside creativity justifications, so the coefficient
# answers a plain question: when someone justified a creativity score by
# pointing at visible detail, was the score higher or lower? Fitting it with
# the same model as concept talk is what lets the components be compared.
creativity_execution_table <- run_or_report(
  "4.2 creativity ~ execution talk, mixed-effects model",
  function() {
    res <- fit_mixed(rating ~ says_detail + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
                     creativity_human,
                     step = "4.2 creativity ~ execution talk")
    tidy_mixed(res) %>%
      mutate(model = "rating ~ execution talk (visible detail)") %>%
      relocate(model) %>%
      mutate(arm = "Human", dimension = "creativity")
  }
)

if (!is.null(creativity_execution_table)) {
  print(creativity_execution_table)
  write_csv(creativity_execution_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_creativity_execution_lmm.csv"))
}

# Save the concept fit alongside the others, so a reviewer can re-inspect it

if (!is.null(creativity_concept_fit)) {
  saveRDS(creativity_concept_fit,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_creativity_concept.rds"))
```

## 4.3 The novelty component

```{r novelty-scope}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE LEGAL POINT, stated once so the statistics have something to answer to.
#
# Copyright asks for independent creation plus a minimal spark of creativity.
# It does not ask whether the work is new to the world: two people who
# independently paint the same sunset each own their own painting. Novelty,
# in the sense of "not previously known", is a patent requirement.
#
# So if lay raters lower their creativity score for work that strikes them as
# familiar, derivative or generic, they are applying a test copyright rejects.
# That would be a finding about the gap between lay intuition and doctrine,
# and it is measurable here because the flags include a three-way
# prior-exposure category:
#
#   asserted:  the response says the work looks familiar, seen before, generic
#   negated:   the response explicitly denies it ("I've never seen anything
#              like this"), which is a rater volunteering that novelty mattered
#              to them, in the positive direction
#   neither:   the response says nothing either way
#
# The three-way split matters. If we collapsed "negated" into "neither" we
# would be treating an explicit novelty claim as silence, and the asserted-
# minus-neither difference would be measured against a contaminated baseline.
#
# WHY THIS SITS INSIDE SECTION 4 RATHER THAN STANDING ALONE. Asking whether
# raters penalised familiarity is asking what one of the three candidate
# meanings of "creativity" was worth to them. Reported on its own it looks like
# a separate curiosity about novelty; reported here it is one component of the
# denotation question, and the component that carries the sharpest doctrinal
# point: that lay judgment may import a patent standard into a copyright one.
#
# Unlike 4.1, 4.2 and 4.5, this component reads both arms. The preregistration
# (section 9 of that document) estimates the association between the
# prior-exposure category and the creativity rating within each condition
# separately, with random intercepts for participant and for image, and says
# that the association pooled across conditions is not reported as evidence
# for anything. So 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 report the human arm and the AI arm as two
# separate estimates. The reason the pooled version cannot stand in for them
# is in 4.3.3: the AI label independently lowers creativity ratings, and if
# it also changes how often familiarity is raised, a pooled association can
# appear with no within-person relationship behind it. A pooled model with
# the arm as a covariate is still fitted, and deposited beside the per-arm
# ones, as supplementary description only. Fitting inside one arm keeps the
# arm out of the estimate but does not by itself make it a within-person
# estimate, and 4.3.4 splits each per-arm association into its within-person
# and between-person parts.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
creativity_all %>%
  count(Type, prior_exposure) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = prior_exposure, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

### 4.3.1 Average creativity rating in each prior-exposure category

```{r novelty-means}
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_means.csv"))

novelty_means <- creativity_all %>%
  group_by(prior_exposure) %>%
  summarise(
    n_responses    = n(),
    n_participants = n_distinct(id),
    mean_rating    = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rating      = sd(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
novelty_means

# Split by arm as well. The AI label itself lowers creativity ratings, and a
# reader will want to know whether the familiarity gap is the label effect
# under another name. The registered estimates in 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 are
# computed within each arm, so the label effect cannot enter them; this table
# holds the raw means behind those estimates.
novelty_means_by_arm <- creativity_all %>%
  group_by(Type, prior_exposure) %>%
  summarise(
    n_responses = n(),
    mean_rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rating   = sd(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
novelty_means_by_arm

write_csv(bind_rows(
  novelty_means %>% mutate(arm = "both arms pooled") %>% relocate(arm),
  novelty_means_by_arm %>% mutate(arm = as.character(Type)) %>%
    select(arm, prior_exposure, n_responses, mean_rating, sd_rating)
), file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_means.csv"))
```

### 4.3.2 The asserted-minus-neither difference, with a resampled interval

```{r novelty-contrast}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The raw difference for this question: how many rating points lower is a
# creativity score when the justification says the work looks familiar,
# compared with a justification that says nothing about familiarity?
#
# Computed as a difference in means with a participant-resampled interval, so
# it is readable without reference to any model, and computed within each arm
# separately, because that is the estimate the preregistration names: a
# within-condition difference that the gap between the two arms' means cannot
# manufacture. The pooled-arm difference is computed as well and deposited in
# the same table, labelled as such, as supplementary description; it is not
# the reported estimate. The models in 4.3.3 then add the random intercepts;
# if a raw difference and its model disagree, believe the model and say why.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c(
  "study1_text_novelty_contrast.csv",
  "study1_text_novelty_contrast_effort.csv",
  "study1_text_novelty_contrast_both.csv"
)))

exposure_diff_fun <- function(d) {
  m_asserted <- mean(d$rating[d$prior_exposure == "asserted"], na.rm = TRUE)
  m_neither  <- mean(d$rating[d$prior_exposure == "neither"],  na.rm = TRUE)
  m_negated  <- mean(d$rating[d$prior_exposure == "negated"],  na.rm = TRUE)
  c(
    mean_asserted            = m_asserted,
    mean_neither             = m_neither,
    mean_negated             = m_negated,
    asserted_minus_neither   = m_asserted - m_neither,
    negated_minus_neither    = m_negated  - m_neither
  )
}

# One resampled contrast per arm, then the pooled one, on whichever dimension
# is passed in. The arm and role columns are what tell the three blocks of
# rows apart in the deposited table; the per-arm rows come first because they
# are the registered ones.
exposure_contrast_by_arm <- function(d, dim_label) {
  bind_rows(
    lapply(TYPE_LEVELS, function(arm_name) {
      boot_by_participant(d %>% filter(Type == arm_name), exposure_diff_fun) %>%
        mutate(arm = arm_name, role = "registered, within arm")
    }),
    boot_by_participant(d, exposure_diff_fun) %>%
      mutate(arm = "both arms pooled",
             role = "supplementary description, pooled")
  ) %>%
    mutate(dimension = dim_label) %>%
    relocate(dimension, arm, role)
}

novelty_contrast <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.2 asserted-minus-neither creativity difference with resampled CI, within each arm",
  function() exposure_contrast_by_arm(creativity_all, "creativity")
)
if (!is.null(novelty_contrast)) {
  for (arm_name in TYPE_LEVELS) {
    cat("\n", arm_name, " arm, creativity:\n", sep = "")
    novelty_contrast %>% filter(arm == arm_name) %>%
      select(quantity, estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>% print()
  }
  cat("\nBoth arms pooled, creativity (supplementary description only):\n")
  novelty_contrast %>% filter(!arm %in% TYPE_LEVELS) %>%
    select(quantity, estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>% print()
  write_csv(novelty_contrast,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_contrast.csv"))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE SPECIFICITY COMPARISON.
#
# Apply the same rule to effort justifications. The prior-exposure pattern
# has no special claim on effort: saying a work looks generic is an argument
# about originality, not about labour. So if the familiarity gap is specific
# to creativity, that is evidence that raters apply a novelty test to the
# creativity construct. If familiarity lowers both ratings equally, the
# simpler reading is that people who dislike a picture say so in every way
# available to them, and the novelty account is not needed.
#
# This comparison decides whether the novelty finding is specific to
# creativity, so it is run with the same code as the creativity contrast.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
novelty_contrast_effort <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.2 same rule applied to effort justifications, within each arm (specificity check)",
  function() exposure_contrast_by_arm(effort_all, "effort")
)
if (!is.null(novelty_contrast_effort)) {
  for (arm_name in TYPE_LEVELS) {
    cat("\n", arm_name, " arm, effort:\n", sep = "")
    novelty_contrast_effort %>% filter(arm == arm_name) %>%
      select(quantity, estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>% print()
  }
  cat("\nBoth arms pooled, effort (supplementary description only):\n")
  novelty_contrast_effort %>% filter(!arm %in% TYPE_LEVELS) %>%
    select(quantity, estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>% print()
  write_csv(novelty_contrast_effort,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_novelty_contrast_effort.csv"))
}

# Both together, as the one table the manuscript will cite. The rows to cite
# are the per-arm ones; the pooled rows sit beneath them as description.
if (!is.null(novelty_contrast) && !is.null(novelty_contrast_effort)) {
  novelty_contrast_both <- bind_rows(novelty_contrast, novelty_contrast_effort)
  write_csv(novelty_contrast_both,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_contrast_both.csv"))
  novelty_contrast_both %>%
    filter(quantity == "asserted_minus_neither") %>%
    select(dimension, arm, role, estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi, n_valid) %>%
    print()
}
```

### 4.3.3 The mixed-effects model

```{r novelty-lmm}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE REGISTERED MODEL, fitted once inside each arm:
#
#   rating ~ prior_exposure + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# on that arm's creativity responses, with "neither" as the reference category
# so the coefficient labelled prior_exposureasserted reads as "rating points
# lower, within this arm, for a response that called the work familiar".
# The preregistration (section 9 of that document) specifies the estimate this
# way, within each condition separately, so that the gap between the two
# arms' means cannot manufacture it. Fitting inside one arm means the arm
# cannot enter the model at all, which is a stronger guarantee than adjusting
# for it.
#
# What this model does not deliver is a purely within-person association,
# which is what the preregistration's wording asks for. The random intercept
# gives each participant their own baseline and each image its own, but the
# familiarity categories enter uncentred, so the coefficient mixes two
# things: whether a person rates an image lower when they call that image
# familiar, and whether people who call works familiar more often rate lower
# across the board. It is kept here as description, an arm-specific
# mixed-model association, and 4.3.4 below fits the decomposition that
# separates the two parts and reads the within-person part.
#
# A prior-exposure category with no responses behind it within an arm is
# dropped before fitting rather than left in as an all-zero column, and the
# categories present are recorded beside the estimates.
#
# The same model is then fitted to effort, again inside each arm, as the
# specificity comparison.
#
# THE SUPPLEMENTARY MODEL, fitted on both arms together:
#
#   rating ~ prior_exposure + Type + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# with the arm as a covariate, so its familiarity coefficient is a within-arm
# comparison averaged over the two arms. It is kept because a reader will
# want to see whether it agrees with the two per-arm estimates, and it is
# deposited and labelled as description; the preregistration says the pooled
# association is not reported as evidence, and it is not.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(
  file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_text_novelty_by_arm.csv",
                            "study1_text_novelty_lmm.csv",
                            "study1_text_novelty_emmeans.csv")),
  file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, c("study1_text_novelty_by_arm_fits.rds",
                               "study1_text_novelty_creativity.rds",
                               "study1_text_novelty_effort.rds",
                               "study1_text_effort_detail.rds"))
)

# The registered model, inside one arm and one dimension.
fit_novelty_within_arm <- function(dim_name, arm_name) {
  d <- dat %>%
    filter(dimension == dim_name, Type == arm_name, !is.na(rating)) %>%
    mutate(
      prior_exposure = droplevels(relevel(factor(prior_exposure,
                                                 levels = EXPOSURE_LEVELS),
                                          ref = "neither"))
    )
  res <- fit_mixed(
    rating ~ prior_exposure + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), d,
    step = paste0("4.3.3 ", dim_name, " ~ prior exposure, ", arm_name, " arm")
  )
  c(res, list(data = d))
}

# The four within-arm fits (two arms by two dimensions), each kept with its
# tidied rows so the fits can be saved and the rows deposited from one object.
novelty_by_arm <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.3 rating ~ prior exposure within each arm, creativity and effort, mixed-effects models",
  function() {
    grid <- expand.grid(arm = TYPE_LEVELS, dimension = DIM_LEVELS,
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    out <- Map(function(dim_name, arm_name) {
      res <- fit_novelty_within_arm(dim_name, arm_name)
      d   <- res$data
      rows <- tidy_mixed(res) %>%
        mutate(
          dimension      = dim_name,
          arm            = arm_name,
          role           = "registered, within arm",
          n_responses    = nrow(d),
          n_participants = n_distinct(d$id),
          n_neither      = sum(d$prior_exposure == "neither"),
          n_asserted     = sum(d$prior_exposure == "asserted"),
          n_negated      = sum(d$prior_exposure == "negated"),
          levels_present = paste(levels(d$prior_exposure), collapse = ", "),
          singular       = res$status == "singular",
          model = paste0("rating ~ prior_exposure + (1 | id) + ",
                         "(1 | stimulus_id), REML, bobyqa, within arm")
        ) %>%
        relocate(dimension, arm, role)
      list(fit = res$fit, status = res$status, rows = rows)
    }, grid$dimension, grid$arm)
    names(out) <- paste(grid$dimension, grid$arm, sep = "_")
    out
  }
)

novelty_by_arm_table <- NULL
if (!is.null(novelty_by_arm)) {
  novelty_by_arm_table <- bind_rows(lapply(novelty_by_arm, `[[`, "rows"))
  for (dim_name in DIM_LEVELS) {
    for (arm_name in TYPE_LEVELS) {
      cat("\n", arm_name, " arm, ", dim_name, " ~ prior exposure:\n", sep = "")
      novelty_by_arm_table %>%
        filter(dimension == dim_name, arm == arm_name) %>%
        select(term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, p.value,
               n_asserted, n_negated, levels_present, singular) %>%
        print(width = Inf)
    }
  }
  write_csv(novelty_by_arm_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_by_arm.csv"))
  saveRDS(lapply(novelty_by_arm, `[[`, "fit"),
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_novelty_by_arm_fits.rds"))
}

# The supplementary pooled model, both arms with the arm as a covariate.
fit_novelty <- function(dim_name) {
  d <- dat %>%
    filter(dimension == dim_name, !is.na(rating)) %>%
    mutate(
      prior_exposure = relevel(factor(prior_exposure,
                                      levels = EXPOSURE_LEVELS),
                               ref = "neither"),
      Type           = relevel(factor(Type, levels = TYPE_LEVELS),
                               ref = "Human")
    )
  fit_mixed(
    rating ~ prior_exposure + Type + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), d,
    step = paste0("4.3.3 ", dim_name, " ~ prior exposure + arm, pooled")
  )
}

novelty_res_creativity <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.3 creativity ~ prior exposure + arm, pooled mixed-effects model (supplementary description)",
  function() fit_novelty("creativity")
)
novelty_res_effort <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.3 effort ~ prior exposure + arm, pooled mixed-effects model (supplementary description, specificity)",
  function() fit_novelty("effort")
)
novelty_fit_creativity <- novelty_res_creativity$fit
novelty_fit_effort     <- novelty_res_effort$fit

novelty_lmm_table <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.3 tidy both pooled prior-exposure models",
  function() {
    bind_rows(
      tidy_mixed(novelty_res_creativity) %>% mutate(dimension = "creativity"),
      tidy_mixed(novelty_res_effort) %>% mutate(dimension = "effort")
    ) %>%
      mutate(arm  = "both arms pooled",
             role = "supplementary description, Type as covariate") %>%
      relocate(dimension, arm, role)
  }
)
if (!is.null(novelty_lmm_table)) {
  cat("\nBoth arms pooled, Type as covariate (supplementary description ",
      "only):\n", sep = "")
  print(novelty_lmm_table)
  write_csv(novelty_lmm_table,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_lmm.csv"))
}

# Model-implied means for the three categories, the form a reader can
# compare with the raw means in 4.3.1 to check that the model has not done
# anything surprising. One block of rows per arm from the registered
# within-arm creativity models, then one from the pooled model, told apart by
# the arm and role columns. A fit whose status does not permit inference
# contributes no rows.
novelty_emm <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.3 estimated marginal means by prior-exposure category, within each arm and pooled",
  function() {
    per_arm <- if (is.null(novelty_by_arm)) tibble() else {
      bind_rows(lapply(TYPE_LEVELS, function(arm_name) {
        cell <- novelty_by_arm[[paste("creativity", arm_name, sep = "_")]]
        if (!cell$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS) return(tibble())
        as_tibble(emmeans::emmeans(cell$fit, ~ prior_exposure)) %>%
          mutate(arm = arm_name, role = "registered, within arm")
      }))
    }
    pooled <- if (!isTRUE(novelty_res_creativity$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS)) {
      tibble()
    } else {
      as_tibble(emmeans::emmeans(novelty_fit_creativity,
                                 ~ prior_exposure)) %>%
        mutate(arm  = "both arms pooled",
               role = "supplementary description, Type as covariate")
    }
    bind_rows(per_arm, pooled) %>%
      mutate(dimension = "creativity") %>%
      relocate(dimension, arm, role)
  }
)
if (!is.null(novelty_emm)) {
  print(novelty_emm)
  write_csv(novelty_emm,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_emmeans.csv"))
}

# Save the two fits so a later notebook or a reviewer can re-inspect them
# without re-running this file.
if (!is.null(novelty_fit_creativity)) {
  saveRDS(novelty_fit_creativity,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_novelty_creativity.rds"))
}
if (!is.null(novelty_fit_effort)) {
  saveRDS(novelty_fit_effort,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_novelty_effort.rds"))

if (!is.null(effort_detail_fit)) {
  saveRDS(effort_detail_fit,
```
