### 4.3.4 The within-person and between-person parts of the familiarity association

```{r novelty-within-between}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THE PREREGISTRATION ASKS FOR, AND WHY 4.3.3 DOES NOT DELIVER IT.
#
# The registered estimand is a within-person association: does a participant
# give a lower creativity rating to the images they call familiar than to the
# images they say nothing about? The model in 4.3.3 enters the familiarity
# category as it stands. A participant who calls works familiar in six of ten
# explanations and a participant who never does differ in two ways at once,
# image by image and overall, and the single coefficient averages the two.
# If people who reach for familiarity talk also rate everything lower, that
# between-person difference flows into the coefficient however the random
# intercept is set.
#
# THE DECOMPOSITION. Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator (asserted
# familiarity, denied familiarity), and each indicator is split into two
# columns. The between-person column is the participant's own share of
# explanations in that category, the same number on all ten of their rows.
# The within-person column is the indicator minus that share, so it is
# positive on the explanations where the participant raised the category and
# negative on the rest, and it averages to exactly zero for every
# participant. Both columns enter one model, fitted inside each arm:
#
#   rating ~ asserted_within + asserted_between
#            + negated_within + negated_between
#            + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# Because the within column carries no difference between participants, its
# coefficient is estimated only from each person's own contrast between
# their explanations. It is the within-person association, in rating points:
# how much lower a response that called the work familiar is rated than the
# same person's other responses. The between column's coefficient is the
# between-person association: the difference in a participant's ratings
# that goes with their share of familiarity talk running from none of their
# explanations to all of them, so a tenth of it goes with one more explanation
# in ten. This form of model is sometimes called the within-between or
# hybrid model, and it keeps the image intercept the registered model has.
#
# The model is fitted for creativity, which is the registered association,
# and for effort as the specificity comparison of 4.3.2. A category with no
# responses in an arm, or one that never varies inside any participant,
# leaves its columns out, and the terms that remain are recorded. Each fit
# goes through fit_mixed() and carries its status. Neither part is a cause:
# the explanation was written after the rating.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_within_between.csv"))

fit_novelty_within_between <- function(dim_name, arm_name) {
  d <- dat %>%
    filter(dimension == dim_name, Type == arm_name, !is.na(rating)) %>%
    mutate(asserted = as.numeric(prior_exposure == "asserted"),
           negated  = as.numeric(prior_exposure == "negated")) %>%
    group_by(id) %>%
    mutate(asserted_between = mean(asserted),
           negated_between  = mean(negated)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(asserted_within = asserted - asserted_between,
           negated_within  = negated  - negated_between)

  # Keep a category's two columns only when both carry information: some
  # participant raised it on some but not all of their explanations (so the
  # within column varies), and participants differ in how often (so the
  # between column varies).
  keep <- character()
  for (cat_name in c("asserted", "negated")) {
    if (sd(d[[paste0(cat_name, "_within")]]) > 0 &&
        sd(d[[paste0(cat_name, "_between")]]) > 0) {
      keep <- c(keep, paste0(cat_name, c("_within", "_between")))
    }
  }
  if (length(keep) == 0) stop("No familiarity category varies in the ",
                              arm_name, " arm's ", dim_name, " responses.")
  f <- stats::as.formula(paste0("rating ~ ", paste(keep, collapse = " + "),
                                " + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)"))
  res <- fit_mixed(f, d, step = paste0("4.3.4 ", dim_name,
                                       " ~ familiarity within and between, ",
                                       arm_name, " arm"))
  tidy_mixed(res) %>%
    filter(is.na(term) | term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(
      dimension      = dim_name,
      arm            = arm_name,
      role           = if (dim_name == "creativity")
                         "registered association, split into its two parts"
                       else "specificity comparison, description",
      category       = sub("_(within|between)$", "", term),
      part           = ifelse(grepl("_within$", term), "within-person",
                              "between-person"),
      n_responses    = nrow(d),
      n_participants = n_distinct(d$id),
      n_asserted     = sum(d$asserted),
      n_negated      = sum(d$negated),
      n_participants_asserted = n_distinct(d$id[d$asserted == 1]),
      n_participants_negated  = n_distinct(d$id[d$negated == 1]),
      terms_present  = paste(keep, collapse = ", "),
      model = paste0(deparse(f, width.cutoff = 500L),
                     ", REML, bobyqa, within arm; *_within is the indicator ",
                     "minus the participant's share, *_between the share")
    ) %>%
    relocate(dimension, arm, role, category, part, term)
}

novelty_within_between <- run_or_report(
  "4.3.4 familiarity and the rating, within-person and between-person parts, each arm",
  function() {
    grid <- expand.grid(arm = TYPE_LEVELS, dimension = DIM_LEVELS,
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    bind_rows(Map(fit_novelty_within_between, grid$dimension, grid$arm))
  }
)

if (!is.null(novelty_within_between)) {
  novelty_within_between %>%
    select(dimension, arm, category, part, estimate, std.error, conf.low,
           conf.high, p.value, status) %>%
    print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
  write_csv(novelty_within_between,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_novelty_within_between.csv"))

  # The within-person part in words, which is the registered quantity.
  for (dim_name in DIM_LEVELS) {
    for (arm_name in TYPE_LEVELS) {
      w <- novelty_within_between %>%
        filter(dimension == dim_name, arm == arm_name, part == "within-person")
      for (i in seq_len(nrow(w))) {
        cat(arm_name, " arm, ", dim_name, ", ",
            ifelse(w$category[i] == "asserted", "calling the work familiar",
                   "denying that it was familiar"),
            ": within-person association ",
            sprintf("%+.3f", w$estimate[i]), " rating points (95% interval ",
            ifelse(is.na(w$conf.low[i]), "not reported, see the status",
                   sprintf("%+.3f to %+.3f", w$conf.low[i], w$conf.high[i])),
            "; status ", w$status[i], ").\n", sep = "")
      }
    }
  }
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the within-person rows for creativity in each arm. They say
# whether a person rated lower the particular images they called familiar.
# The between-person rows say whether people who use familiarity talk more
# often rate lower in general; a large between-person coefficient beside a
# small within-person one is the pattern the uncentred model of 4.3.3 would
# have folded into one number.
```

## 4.4 What an association between the writing and the rating can and cannot show

```{r denotation-caution, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("
Every model in this section and in section 3 relates something a participant
wrote to a number the same participant had just given, with one exception.
The registered comparisons in 3.1.1 and 4.1.1 relate one kind of writing to
another and never read the rating, which is why they can be tests where the
rest of these two sections is description. Everything else here shares the
limit that follows. The justification was written immediately after the
rating it explains. That ordering rules out one reading and permits another,
and the difference matters enough to state here rather than leave to a
limitations paragraph.

**What these models cannot show.** They cannot show that the writing caused the
rating. A person who has already decided on a 4 will then reach for a reason,
and the reason they reach for is chosen with the 4 already in hand. So an
association between concept talk and higher creativity scores is equally
consistent with 'thinking about the idea led this person to a high score' and
with 'this person gave a high score and then explained it in terms of the
idea'. Nothing in this design separates those two, and no amount of statistical
control inside a single person's response can separate them, because the
control would be applied to data generated after the fact. What is missing
is *temporal ordering*: the reasoning would have to be recorded before the
number was fixed, and the instrument does not record it that way.

**What these models can show.** They show what the word denoted for the people
who used it. If the participants who justified creativity by pointing at an
idea are the participants who gave higher creativity scores, then for those
raters 'creative' picked out works with ideas behind them, whatever the causal
order in which that pairing was assembled. Denotation is the question section 4
asks. It is a smaller claim than causation, and it is the claim the
doctrinal argument needs: the paper's point is about what the rated
construct consists of, not about what moves it.

**What the across-image correlation in 4.5 can and cannot show.** Sections
4.2 and 4.3 compare individual responses. Section 4.5 compares *images*: it
asks whether the artworks that drew more concept talk are the artworks that
received higher average creativity ratings, averaging over all the people
who saw each one. Every participant in the arm rated all ten images, so a
person's general habits, such as rating every image high or writing about
ideas in every response, add the same amount to every image's average and
cannot by themselves produce a relationship across images. That is what the
correlation removes: differences between people in their overall level.

It does not remove the problem set out above, that each justification was
written after its rating. If raters who have just given a high score tend to
explain it in terms of the idea, then
whichever images are rated higher, for whatever reason, will collect more
concept talk, and the across-image correlation will appear even if no idea
in any picture moved any rating. The habit need not be coordinated across
the ten pictures; it only has to be applied rating by rating. A correlation
at the image level is therefore consistent with both readings given above,
and it cannot say whether the images differ in a feature that raters noticed
and scored, or differ only in their ratings with the talk following the
score. What it supports is the same kind of denotation claim as the
response-level models, stated for images rather than for single responses.
The same analysis is run for effort in section 3.3, under the same limit.

The correlation is computed over ten points, so its interval is wide and it
is reported as wide.
")
```

## 4.5 Across the ten images, does concept talk track the creativity rating?

```{r creativity-image-correlation}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The mirror of section 3.3. Section 4.4 sets out what this correlation can
# and cannot show.
#
# For each of the ten artworks, compute two numbers in the human arm:
#   (1) the proportion of creativity justifications that mention the idea,
#       meaning or story behind the work;
#   (2) the average creativity rating.
# Then correlate the two across the ten images.
#
# If images that provoke concept talk are also the images that get high
# creativity ratings, then "creativity" as measured by this instrument is
# largely a judgment about whether the picture has an idea in it. Such a
# judgment is close to what Feist's minimal spark is meant to pick out, and it
# would support the mapping. If instead the images that get high creativity
# ratings are the ones that provoke execution talk, the creativity rating is
# reading the surface much as the effort rating does, and the two constructs
# are less separate than the argument needs.
#
# So the execution version of the same correlation is computed alongside it, on
# identical terms. Reporting only the one that came out better would make the
# comparison meaningless.
#
# The interval comes from resampling participants, not images: both per-image
# numbers are recomputed inside each replicate from the drawn participants, so
# the interval reflects the uncertainty that comes from having sampled these
# 56 people. It does not reflect uncertainty from having chosen these ten
# images. Ten images are too few to resample, and the paper should say so.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c(
  "study1_text_image_concept_creativity.csv",
  "study1_text_creativity_image_corr.csv",
  "study1_text_creativity_image_corr_rank.csv"
)))

image_stats_creativity <- creativity_human %>%
  group_by(stimulus_id, stimulus_type, stimulus_num) %>%
  summarise(
    n_responses      = n(),
    concept_rate     = mean(says_concept),
    execution_rate   = mean(says_detail),
    novelty_rate     = mean(prior_exposure != "neither"),
    mean_creativity  = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(stimulus_type, stimulus_num)

image_stats_creativity
write_csv(image_stats_creativity,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_image_concept_creativity.csv"))

creativity_image_corr <- run_or_report(
  "4.5 image-level correlations, concept- and execution-talk rate vs mean creativity rating",
  function() {
    concept_fun <- function(d) {
      s <- d %>%
        group_by(stimulus_id) %>%
        summarise(concept_rate = mean(says_concept),
                  mean_creativity = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
                  .groups = "drop")
      if (nrow(s) < 3 || sd(s$concept_rate) == 0 ||
          sd(s$mean_creativity) == 0) return(NA_real_)
      c(pearson_r_concept = suppressWarnings(
        cor(s$concept_rate, s$mean_creativity, method = "pearson")))
    }
    execution_fun <- function(d) {
      s <- d %>%
        group_by(stimulus_id) %>%
        summarise(execution_rate = mean(says_detail),
                  mean_creativity = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
                  .groups = "drop")
      if (nrow(s) < 3 || sd(s$execution_rate) == 0 ||
          sd(s$mean_creativity) == 0) return(NA_real_)
      c(pearson_r_execution = suppressWarnings(
        cor(s$execution_rate, s$mean_creativity, method = "pearson")))
    }
    bind_rows(
      boot_by_participant(creativity_human, concept_fun),
      boot_by_participant(creativity_human, execution_fun)
    ) %>%
      mutate(
        arm       = "Human",
        dimension = "creativity",
        n_images  = nrow(image_stats_creativity),
        note      = "10 images; interval reflects participant sampling only"
      )
  }
)

if (!is.null(creativity_image_corr)) {
  print(creativity_image_corr)
  write_csv(creativity_image_corr,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_creativity_image_corr.csv"))
}

# The rank correlations as well, for the same reason as in section 3.3: with
# ten points one unusual image can drag a Pearson correlation around, and
# Spearman's rank version, which uses only the order of the ten values and not
# their spacing, is much less sensitive to that.
creativity_image_corr_spearman <- run_or_report(
  "4.5 image-level rank correlations (Spearman)",
  function() {
    rank_one <- function(x, label) {
      ct <- suppressWarnings(
        cor.test(x, image_stats_creativity$mean_creativity,
                 method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
      )
      tibble(
        quantity = label,
        estimate = unname(ct$estimate),
        p_value  = ct$p.value,
        n_images = nrow(image_stats_creativity)
      )
    }
    bind_rows(
      rank_one(image_stats_creativity$concept_rate,   "spearman_rho_concept"),
      rank_one(image_stats_creativity$execution_rate, "spearman_rho_execution")
    )
  }
)
if (!is.null(creativity_image_corr_spearman)) {
  print(creativity_image_corr_spearman)
  write_csv(creativity_image_corr_spearman,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_creativity_image_corr_rank.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the two correlations side by side. Which of concept talk and
# execution talk tracks the creativity rating across images is the between-image
# form of the denotation question. Differences between people in overall level
# cannot produce it, but a habit of explaining high scores with one kind of
# talk can, so it does not answer the point in section 4.4 that each
# justification was written after its rating.
```

---

# 5. The belief audit: machine talk in the human-attribution arm

The human-attribution vignette is a cover story: every one of the ten images
was in fact machine-generated, and the participants told a person made them
were told something untrue. The instrument carries no manipulation check (no
item asked anyone who they thought made the work), so the written
justifications are the only audit available.

The audit can deliver two counts and their uncertainty. Each count is the
share of participants in the human-attribution arm whose writing brought a
machine into the picture, under one of two rules. Neither count measures
disbelief. A participant who wrote nothing about a machine may have been
suspicious and not said so, and nothing here can tell that person from one
who accepted the vignette entirely. A participant who wrote that a picture
looks machine-made may have been describing its appearance while still
taking the vignette at its word.

The counts come from two fixed search patterns that differ in what they
require of a sentence. The broad count is of participants with at least one
response that mentions machines or prompting. Its rule, `says_prompt`, fires
on any mention of a machine, an AI, or the act of prompting or generating,
whatever the sentence goes on to say about it. The narrow count is of
participants with at least one response that states the work is or looks
machine-made. It reads the machine-authorship rule, `says_machine_made`,
through `machine_made_reading`. It keeps the responses in which the
machine-making phrase was asserted, plainly or as an impression ("probably
AI", "looks AI generated"), and sets aside those in which every such phrase
was negated ("doesn't look AI generated", "AI didn't make this") or
conditional ("if a computer made this"). A sentence that names a digital tool
without saying the tool made the work ("done in Photoshop") sits inside the
broad count and outside the narrow one. A digital tool is what the
human-attribution vignette said the artist used, and that difference is the
reason for keeping both counts. Each rule is applied identically to every
response and printed in full in `tables/text_rules.txt`, and neither count
depends on anyone reading an individual sentence. Section 5.3 gives both
counts an interval from resampling participants. Sections 5.4 and 5.5 then
refit the primary models without the participants in the narrow count. They
set that refit beside a matched removal: the effect size recomputed after
removing random groups of the same size with nearly the same average effort
rating, which shows how far such a removal moves it.

## 5.1 The broad count: mentions machines or prompting

```{r belief-audit-count}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The broad rule is `says_prompt`: a fixed search pattern that fires when a
# response mentions prompting, typing, generating, or names a machine or an
# AI. In the AI-attribution arm that is plain description and is reported as
# such in section 6. In the human-attribution arm it is a leak: the
# participant was told a person made the work and wrote about a machine
# anyway. It fires on a sentence about a digital tool as readily as on a
# sentence about machine authorship, so its count is a count of mentions;
# 5.2 supplies the narrower count of statements.
#
# The unit that matters is the participant, not the response. One stray
# mention in twenty responses means something different from ten, so both the
# participant count and the response count are reported, and the per-person
# breakdown is written out beside them in 5.2.
#
# The two labels below name the two sets everywhere in this section, in the
# deposited tables and in the console, so any row can be traced to the rule
# that produced it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

BROAD_LABEL  <- "broad: mentions machines or prompting (says_prompt)"
NARROW_LABEL <- paste0("narrow: states the work is or looks machine-made ",
                       "(machine_made_reading = asserted)")

human_ids <- sort(unique(dat$id[dat$Type == "Human"]))

# The count for one rule, as a function of the joined frame and the flag
# column, so that the broad count and the narrow count come from one piece of
# arithmetic.
leakage_count_for <- function(dat_x, flag_col, set_label) {
  human_x   <- dat_x %>% filter(Type == "Human")
  matches_x <- human_x %>% filter(.data[[flag_col]])
  ids_x     <- sort(unique(matches_x$id))
  tibble(
    set                    = set_label,
    flag                   = flag_col,
    n_human_participants   = n_distinct(human_x$id),
    n_leak_participants    = length(ids_x),
    pct_leak_participants  = length(ids_x) / n_distinct(human_x$id),
    n_human_responses      = nrow(human_x),
    n_leak_responses       = nrow(matches_x),
    pct_leak_responses     = nrow(matches_x) / nrow(human_x)
  )
}

belief_broad     <- dat %>% filter(Type == "Human", says_prompt)
belief_ids_broad <- sort(unique(belief_broad$id))

leakage_count_broad <- leakage_count_for(dat, "says_prompt", BROAD_LABEL)
leakage_count_broad

cat("\nBroad count. In the human-attribution arm, ", nrow(belief_broad),
    " of ", sum(dat$Type == "Human"), " responses, from ",
    length(belief_ids_broad), " of ", length(human_ids), " participants (",
    pct(length(belief_ids_broad) / length(human_ids)),
    "), mentioned machines or prompting.\n", sep = "")
```

## 5.2 The narrow count: states the work is or looks machine-made

```{r belief-audit-narrow}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The narrow count reads the machine-authorship rule, `says_machine_made`,
# which fires when a response mentions a machine MAKING the work. In words: a
# machine noun (AI, computer, algorithm, program, generator, a named image
# generator, and the like) followed closely by a making verb ("the AI
# generated this"); or a making verb followed by "by", "with", "using" or
# "from" and a machine noun ("made with an AI"); or a compound such as
# "ai-generated", "computer generated" or "machine made". A sentence in which
# a person is the agent of tool use ("Alex used an AI", "the artist used a
# program") does not fire it, and neither does "AI" as a mere subject of
# discussion with no making verb. The exact pattern is printed in
# tables/text_rules.txt beside the other rules, and its matched and unmatched
# examples are in tables/text_audit_matches.txt.
#
# The flag fires on a mention whichever way it points, and a denial is a
# mention: "this does not look AI generated" fires it. So the count is taken
# from machine_made_reading, which the notebook sets to "asserted" when at
# least one matched phrase is stated, plainly or as an impression ("probably
# AI", "looks AI generated"), and to "not_asserted" when every matched phrase
# has a negating word inside it or in the stretch of its clause before it, or
# sits in a clause that opens with if, whether, unless or even if. Only the
# asserted responses count.
#
# WHY THIS IS THE SET THE REFITS USE. A participant who wrote "done in
# Photoshop" described a tool, which is what the human-attribution vignette
# said the artist used. A participant who wrote "this was clearly generated by
# an AI" stated something the vignette did not say about who made the work.
# The narrow count keeps the second and not the first, so its participants
# are the ones who stated that the work is or looks machine-made, and
# sections 5.4 and 5.5 remove exactly them.
#
# The narrow rule needs a machine noun and a making verb, and the broad rule
# needs only a machine or prompting word, so a response in the narrow count
# is expected to be one the broad rule matches too. How many fall outside the
# broad set is printed as a check on that expectation rather than asserted:
# the two rules are written independently, and a machine noun the narrow rule
# knows and the broad rule does not would put a response in the narrow count
# alone.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c(
  "study1_text_leakage_count.csv",
  "study1_text_leakage_per_participant.csv",
  "study1_text_belief_audit_counts.csv"
)))

belief_narrow     <- dat %>% filter(Type == "Human", states_machine_made)
belief_ids_narrow <- sort(unique(belief_narrow$id))

leakage_count_narrow <- leakage_count_for(dat, "states_machine_made",
                                          NARROW_LABEL)
leakage_count_narrow

cat("\nNarrow count. In the human-attribution arm, ", nrow(belief_narrow),
    " of ", sum(dat$Type == "Human"), " responses, from ",
    length(belief_ids_narrow), " of ", length(human_ids), " participants (",
    pct(length(belief_ids_narrow) / length(human_ids)),
    "), stated that the work is or looks machine-made.\n", sep = "")

n_not_asserted <- sum(dat$Type == "Human" &
                        dat$machine_made_reading == "not_asserted")
cat("Human-arm responses that mention a machine making the work only in a ",
    "negated or conditional phrase, and so sit outside the narrow count: ",
    n_not_asserted, ".\n", sep = "")

n_narrow_only <- sum(dat$Type == "Human" & dat$states_machine_made &
                       !dat$says_prompt)
cat("Responses in the narrow count that the broad rule did not also match: ",
    n_narrow_only, ".\n", sep = "")

# Both counts in one deposited table.
leakage_count <- bind_rows(leakage_count_broad, leakage_count_narrow)
leakage_count
write_csv(leakage_count,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_leakage_count.csv"))

# How many responses each flagged participant wrote that way, under each
# rule. A participant with responses in the broad count and none in the
# narrow one named a machine or a tool without ever stating it made the work.
leak_per_participant <- dat %>%
  filter(Type == "Human", says_prompt | states_machine_made) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_broad_responses  = sum(says_prompt),
    n_narrow_responses = sum(states_machine_made),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_narrow_responses), desc(n_broad_responses))
print(leak_per_participant, n = Inf)
write_csv(leak_per_participant,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_leakage_per_participant.csv"))

# The two participant counts side by side, which is the table the manuscript
# cites.
belief_audit_counts <- tibble(
  set                    = c(BROAD_LABEL, NARROW_LABEL),
  flag                   = c("says_prompt",
                             "machine_made_reading == asserted"),
  n_participants_flagged = c(length(belief_ids_broad),
                             length(belief_ids_narrow)),
  n_human_participants   = length(human_ids),
  rate                   = n_participants_flagged / n_human_participants,
  n_responses_flagged    = c(nrow(belief_broad), nrow(belief_narrow)),
  n_human_responses      = sum(dat$Type == "Human"),
  reading                = c("mentions machines or prompting",
                             "states the work is or looks machine-made"),
  note = c("fires on any machine, prompting or generating word",
           paste0("machine-authorship phrase asserted; negated and ",
                  "conditional phrases set aside"))
)
belief_audit_counts
write_csv(belief_audit_counts,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_belief_audit_counts.csv"))
```

## 5.3 The two rates, with intervals from resampling participants

```{r belief-audit-rate-ci}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A bare count invites a reader to treat it as exact. It is not: the human-arm
# participants are a sample, and a different sample of the same size would
# have produced a different number. The interval says how much each rate
# would move, and both rates get one.
#
# It is computed with boot_by_participant() from section 2.5, the same
# resampling routine every other interval in this file uses, and the input is
# a data frame with one row per participant rather than one row per response.
# The statistic is a participant-level rate, so a participant drawn twice by
# the bootstrap must count twice. Given the response-level frame, the twenty
# rows of a twice-drawn person would arrive carrying the same identifier, and
# any grouping by participant would collapse them back to one, undoing the
# resampling without notice. With one row per participant, the mean over rows
# is exactly the rate wanted, with duplicates counted as duplicates.
#
# The interval is a percentile interval on 2,000 resamples, seed 20260421.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_belief_audit_rate_ci.csv"))

# One row per human-arm participant, saying whether any of their responses
# tripped each rule.
belief_participant_frame <- function(dat_x) {
  dat_x %>%
    filter(Type == "Human") %>%
    group_by(id) %>%
    summarise(
      named_machine_broad  = any(says_prompt),
      named_machine_narrow = any(states_machine_made),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

belief_participant_level <- belief_participant_frame(dat)

belief_rate_ci <- run_or_report(
  "5.3 belief-audit rates with participant-resampled intervals, broad and narrow",
  function() {
    bind_rows(
      boot_by_participant(
        belief_participant_level,
        function(d) c(rate = mean(d$named_machine_broad))
      ) %>%
        mutate(set = BROAD_LABEL, flag = "says_prompt", .before = 1),
      boot_by_participant(
        belief_participant_level,
        function(d) c(rate = mean(d$named_machine_narrow))
      ) %>%
        mutate(set = NARROW_LABEL, flag = "machine_made_reading == asserted",
               .before = 1)
    )
  }
)

if (!is.null(belief_rate_ci)) {
  belief_rate_ci %>%
    mutate(across(c(estimate, ci_lo, ci_hi), ~ pct(.x))) %>%
    print(width = Inf)
  write_csv(belief_rate_ci,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_belief_audit_rate_ci.csv"))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(belief_rate_ci))) {
    cat("\n", belief_rate_ci$set[i], ": ",
        pct(belief_rate_ci$estimate[i]), " of human-arm participants (95% ",
        "interval ", pct(belief_rate_ci$ci_lo[i]), " to ",
        pct(belief_rate_ci$ci_hi[i]), "), from resampling the ",
        length(human_ids), " participants ", B_BOOT, " times.\n", sep = "")
  }
  cat("\nNeither rate measures disbelief. Participants who doubted the ",
      "vignette without writing about it are invisible to both rules, and a ",
      "participant who wrote that a picture looks machine-made may have been ",
      "describing how it looks.\n", sep = "")
}
```

## 5.4 Refitting the primary models without those participants

```{r belief-audit-exclusion-refit}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS IS AND WHAT IT IS NOT.
#
# The full-sample models in Study1_01_Quant.Rmd are the primary analysis. What
# follows is a sensitivity analysis: the same models, on both dimensions, with
# the narrow set from 5.2 set aside, that is, the participants whose writing
# stated that the work is or looks machine-made. It is reported whatever it
# shows, and its estimate is never substituted for the primary one. Section
# 5.5 supplies the comparison that decides whether any difference between the
# two is informative.
#
# TWO QUANTITIES PER DIMENSION, both registered.
#
#   Cohen's d, a difference expressed in standard deviations, computed the
#     one registered way: (human mean minus AI mean) divided by the pooled
#     standard deviation, on PARTICIPANT MEANS, one number per person per
#     dimension averaged over their ten images. Averaging first removes
#     measurement noise that has no place in a between-participant contrast,
#     which is why these values are not comparable to a d computed on raw
#     observations or to the conventional small-medium-large benchmarks. The
#     interval is a stratified percentile bootstrap: participants are resampled
#     within arm, 10,000 times, seed 20260421. That B differs from the 2,000
#     used elsewhere in this file because the registered convention for d
#     fixes 10,000; the proportions in this file are registered at 2,000.
#
#   The primary mixed model, rating ~ attribution * image_kind with random
#     intercepts for participant and for image, refitted; and from it the
#     estimated marginal contrast of human minus AI averaged over image kind.
#     That contrast is the registered quantity, not the raw coefficient: under
#     treatment coding, where each coefficient is measured from a reference
#     level, the raw coefficient is the effect at non-figurative images only.
#     Beside it sits the model-based standardised effect: the
#     contrast divided by the square root of the summed variance components,
#     which is the version comparable to between-subject effect sizes in the
#     surrounding literature.
#
# No correction for multiple tests is applied to the contrasts here, on
# purpose. The registered confirmatory family is the four full-sample
# tests enumerated in the preregistration, and they are corrected together by
# the Holm procedure in Study1_01_Quant.Rmd. These refits are a sensitivity
# analysis outside that family; adding them to it would change the family the
# correction was registered over.
#
# The model is fitted on the full ratings, all 2,220 of them, not on the
# joined frame used elsewhere in this file. The joined frame would drop any
# rating whose response had no row in the flags file, and every rating
# belongs in the primary model whether or not its text was measured. The
# image-kind lookup is rebuilt from the flags file, which is the only place
# in this notebook that records which images are figurative, and it is
# checked for completeness before use.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                        "study1_text_belief_audit_exclusion_refit.csv"))

D_BOOT_B    <- 10000L
D_BOOT_SEED <- 20260421L

# Which of the ten images are figurative. One row per image, asserted complete.
stimulus_kind <- dat %>%
  distinct(stimulus_id, stimulus_type) %>%
  arrange(stimulus_id)
stopifnot(
  nrow(stimulus_kind) == n_distinct(dat$stimulus_id),
  !anyNA(stimulus_kind$stimulus_type)
)

ratings_primary <- ratings %>%
  left_join(stimulus_kind, by = "stimulus_id")
stopifnot(!anyNA(ratings_primary$stimulus_type))

# The registered pooled-standard-deviation formula, reproduced exactly as it
# appears in Study1_01_Quant.Rmd section 9.1.
pooled_d <- function(x_h, x_a) {
  n_h <- length(x_h); n_a <- length(x_a)
  sp  <- sqrt(((n_h - 1) * var(x_h) + (n_a - 1) * var(x_a)) / (n_h + n_a - 2))
  (mean(x_h) - mean(x_a)) / sp
}

# One number per participant per dimension: their average rating over the ten
# images. This is the unit the registered d is computed on.
participant_means <- ratings %>%
  filter(!is.na(rating)) %>%
  group_by(id, Type, dimension) %>%
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop")

# Pre-split those participant means into two named numeric vectors per
# dimension, so that excluding a set of participants is a name lookup rather
# than a filter. Section 5.5 recomputes d several thousand times and this is
# what keeps it quick.
means_by_dimension <- lapply(DIM_LEVELS, function(dim_name) {
  s <- participant_means %>% filter(dimension == dim_name)
  list(
    human = setNames(s$mean_rating[s$Type == "Human"], s$id[s$Type == "Human"]),
    ai    = setNames(s$mean_rating[s$Type == "AI"],    s$id[s$Type == "AI"])
  )
})
names(means_by_dimension) <- DIM_LEVELS

d_excluding <- function(dim_name, exclude_ids = character(0)) {
  v   <- means_by_dimension[[dim_name]]
  x_h <- v$human[setdiff(names(v$human), exclude_ids)]
  x_a <- v$ai[setdiff(names(v$ai), exclude_ids)]
  if (length(x_h) < 3 || length(x_a) < 3) return(NA_real_)
  pooled_d(x_h, x_a)
}

# The registered stratified bootstrap interval for d: resample participants
# within each arm separately, so the two arm sizes stay fixed at what the
# design delivered.
d_with_interval <- function(dim_name, exclude_ids = character(0)) {
  v   <- means_by_dimension[[dim_name]]
  x_h <- unname(v$human[setdiff(names(v$human), exclude_ids)])
  x_a <- unname(v$ai[setdiff(names(v$ai), exclude_ids)])
  stopifnot(length(x_h) > 2, length(x_a) > 2)
  d_obs <- pooled_d(x_h, x_a)
  set.seed(D_BOOT_SEED)   # reset per call so each is independently reproducible
  d_boot <- vapply(seq_len(D_BOOT_B), function(b) {
    pooled_d(sample(x_h, length(x_h), replace = TRUE),
             sample(x_a, length(x_a), replace = TRUE))
  }, numeric(1))
  ci <- unname(quantile(d_boot, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 7))
  tibble(
    dimension = dim_name,
    n_human   = length(x_h),
    n_ai      = length(x_a),
    d         = d_obs,
    d_ci_lo   = ci[1],
    d_ci_hi   = ci[2],
    d_B       = D_BOOT_B,
    d_seed    = D_BOOT_SEED
  )
}

# The primary mixed model, refitted on whatever participants are left, and the
# registered marginal contrast read off it.
primary_refit <- function(dim_name, exclude_ids = character(0)) {
  d_sub <- ratings_primary %>%
    filter(dimension == dim_name, !is.na(rating), !(id %in% exclude_ids)) %>%
    mutate(
      Type          = relevel(factor(Type, levels = TYPE_LEVELS), ref = "Human"),
      stimulus_type = relevel(factor(stimulus_type, levels = STIMTYPE_LEVELS),
                              ref = "NonFigure")
    )

  res <- fit_mixed(
    rating ~ Type * stimulus_type + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), d_sub,
    step = paste0("5.4 primary model refit, ", dim_name, ", ",
                  length(exclude_ids), " participants excluded")
  )
  if (is.null(res$fit)) stop("The primary model refit failed: ", res$note)
  fit      <- res$fit
  eligible <- res$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS

  # emmeans averages over image kind, which is what the registered quantity
  # asks for; adjust = "none" because this is one contrast, and because the
  # registered correction is applied to the confirmatory family elsewhere.
  # emmeans prints "Results may be misleading due to involvement in
  # interactions" here, and that note is expected rather than a warning to act
  # on: it fires whenever a term is averaged over a factor it interacts with,
  # which is precisely the average the registration asks for. The interaction
  # itself is examined in Study1_01_Quant.Rmd, not averaged away here.
  ct <- as.data.frame(
    summary(pairs(emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type), adjust = "none"),
            infer = c(TRUE, TRUE))
  )

  # The model-based standardised effect: the contrast over the square root of
  # every variance the model estimates (participant, image and residual).
  vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(fit))
  total_var <- sum(vc$vcov)

  tibble(
    dimension          = dim_name,
    contrast           = as.character(ct$contrast[1]),
    lmm_estimate       = ct$estimate[1],
    lmm_se             = if (eligible) ct$SE[1] else NA_real_,
    lmm_ci_lo          = if (eligible) ct$lower.CL[1] else NA_real_,
    lmm_ci_hi          = if (eligible) ct$upper.CL[1] else NA_real_,
    lmm_df             = ct$df[1],
    lmm_p              = if (eligible) ct$p.value[1] else NA_real_,
    lmm_d_model_based  = ct$estimate[1] / sqrt(total_var),
    n_participants     = n_distinct(d_sub$id),
    n_observations     = nrow(d_sub),
    singular           = res$status == "singular",
    status             = res$status,
    note               = res$note
  )
}

# Run both quantities for one set of excluded participants, on both dimensions.
audit_refit_for <- function(exclude_ids, set_label) {
  bind_rows(lapply(DIM_LEVELS, function(dim_name) {
    left_join(
      d_with_interval(dim_name, exclude_ids),
      primary_refit(dim_name, exclude_ids),
      by = "dimension"
    ) %>%
      mutate(set = set_label, n_excluded = length(exclude_ids), .before = 1)
  }))
}

# The set removed, stated in words beside the numbers.
cat("Set removed: the narrow set from 5.2, the ", length(belief_ids_narrow),
    " human-arm participants with at least one response that stated the work ",
    "is or looks machine-made (machine_made_reading = asserted). Participants ",
    "who named a machine or a tool without stating it made the work, or who ",
    "mentioned machine making only to deny it, stay in.\n", sep = "")

belief_exclusion_refit <- run_or_report(
  "5.4 primary models refitted without the narrow-set participants",
  function() {
    bind_rows(
      audit_refit_for(character(0),      "full sample"),
      audit_refit_for(belief_ids_narrow, "excluding the narrow set")
    )
  }
)

if (!is.null(belief_exclusion_refit)) {
  belief_exclusion_refit %>%
    select(set, dimension, n_excluded, d, d_ci_lo, d_ci_hi,
           lmm_estimate, lmm_ci_lo, lmm_ci_hi, lmm_p, lmm_d_model_based) %>%
    print(n = Inf)
  write_csv(belief_exclusion_refit,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_belief_audit_exclusion_refit.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the `d` column for each dimension, full sample against
# excluded. The size of the movement is the number section 5.5 puts in
# context; on its own it means nothing, because dropping any comparable set of
# participants from the human arm would move it too.
```

## 5.5 The matched removal that has to accompany that refit

```{r belief-audit-matched-null}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE INFERENCE THE REFIT INVITES, AND WHY IT DOES NOT FOLLOW.
#
# The tempting next step is to drop the participants who wrote about
# machines, refit, see that the human-versus-AI difference grew, and present
# that as evidence that the manipulation worked and that those participants
# were diluting the effect.
#
# That inference does not follow. Participants who write that a work looks
# machine-made also tend to give lower ratings. They sit in the low tail of
# the human arm. Dropping ANY set of low-rating human-arm participants raises
# that arm's mean and therefore widens the human-minus-AI gap, whatever those
# people believed. The effect size would move for a purely arithmetic reason.
#
# So the chunk builds a reference for that arithmetic. Repeatedly:
#   1. draw the same number of human-arm participants at random,
#   2. accept the draw only if the drawn group's average effort rating falls
#      within a calibrated tolerance of the average for the narrow set, the
#      group whose explanations stated the work is or looks machine-made;
#      that is all "matched" means here: a group whose average effort rating
#      is close to the real group's, drawn without regard to what anyone
#      wrote,
#   3. drop them and recompute the effect size on both dimensions.
# Repeat until 2,000 draws have been accepted. That gives the distribution of
# effect sizes produced by dropping a matched but otherwise arbitrary set of
# people, which is the reference the observed value has to be read against.
#
# The matching variable is the participant's average EFFORT rating, and it
# stays the effort rating for both dimensions rather than switching to each
# dimension's own average. That is the registered specification, and holding
# it fixed also keeps the two dimensions' reference distributions built from
# the same accepted draws, so any difference between them comes from the
# ratings rather than from two different sets of draws.
#
# WHAT THE MATCHING HOLDS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. Matching on the average
# effort rating keeps, to within the tolerance and no closer, what the human
# arm's average effort rating becomes once the drawn group is removed; it
# holds nothing else. The creativity average of the drawn groups is free to
# differ from the real group's, and so is the spread of every rating. So the
# effort reference is expected to come out narrower than the creativity one,
# because one input to its effect size is nearly pinned. An observed value
# outside either distribution says that removing these participants
# left an effect size that removing a random group with the same average
# effort rating rarely produces. It does not by itself say why, and the paper
# should describe it as a result that is not compatible with this specified
# reference rather than as an explanation of the change.
#
# CACHING. The accept-reject loop is one of the slowest steps in this file. Its
# result is stored next to the models, keyed on everything that could change
# it: which participants are excluded, the participant means it draws from,
# the number of accepted draws and the seed. If the key matches, the stored
# result is reused and the loop is skipped; if anything has changed, the key
# will not match and the loop runs again. A stale cache therefore cannot be
# read by accident.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The cache holds the distribution for the narrow set. Its key records which
# participants were excluded, so a distribution built for a different set can
# never be read back as this one.
MATCHED_CACHE_PATH <- file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS,
                                "study1_belief_audit_matched_cache_rule.rds")

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_leakage_placebo.csv"))

cached_or_run <- function(cache_path, key, f) {
  if (file.exists(cache_path)) {
    cached <- readRDS(cache_path)
    if (identical(cached$key, key)) {
      cat("Reusing the cached matched-removal distribution from:\n  ",
          cache_path, "\n", sep = "")
      return(cached$value)
    }
    cat("The cached matched-removal distribution does not match the current ",
        "inputs; recomputing.\n", sep = "")
  }
  value <- f()
  saveRDS(list(key = key, value = value), cache_path)
  value
}

matched_removal_null <- function(exclude_ids, set_label) {

  n_drop <- length(exclude_ids)
  if (n_drop == 0) {
    return(tibble(set = set_label,
                  note = "No participants flagged; the comparison is not needed."))
  }

  # The variable we match on: each human-arm participant's average effort
  # rating, and the average of that variable among the participants being
  # dropped.
  effort_human <- means_by_dimension[["effort"]]$human
  pool_ids     <- names(effort_human)
  target       <- mean(effort_human[exclude_ids])

  # CALIBRATING THE MATCHING TOLERANCE. "Matched" needs a number attached to
  # it. We first draw 5,000 unmatched groups, look at how far their average
  # effort rating typically lands from the target, and set the tolerance at
  # the 10th percentile of that distance, so that a draw counts as matched if
  # it is closer than 90% of random draws would be. A floor of 0.05 rating
  # points stops the tolerance from becoming so tight that acceptance is
  # impossibly rare. Both the tolerance and the acceptance rate are reported,
  # so the choice can be checked.
  set.seed(20260421)
  calib <- replicate(5000, {
    abs(mean(effort_human[sample(pool_ids, n_drop)]) - target)
  })
  tol <- max(0.05, unname(quantile(calib, 0.10, names = FALSE)))

  # THE ACCEPT-REJECT LOOP. Draw, test the match, keep it if it passes, until
  # 2,000 have been accepted or the attempt cap is reached. The cap guarantees
  # the chunk terminates; if it is hit, the result records how many draws were
  # accepted, so a thin distribution cannot pass unnoticed.
  set.seed(20260421)
  max_attempts <- 400000L
  d_null       <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B_BOOT, ncol = length(DIM_LEVELS),
                         dimnames = list(NULL, DIM_LEVELS))
  accepted     <- 0L
  attempts     <- 0L

  while (accepted < B_BOOT && attempts < max_attempts) {
    attempts <- attempts + 1L
    cand <- sample(pool_ids, n_drop)
    if (abs(mean(effort_human[cand]) - target) <= tol) {
      accepted <- accepted + 1L
      for (dim_name in DIM_LEVELS) {
        d_null[accepted, dim_name] <- d_excluding(dim_name, cand)
      }
    }
  }
  d_null <- d_null[seq_len(accepted), , drop = FALSE]

  bind_rows(lapply(DIM_LEVELS, function(dim_name) {
    draws      <- d_null[, dim_name]
    draws      <- draws[!is.na(draws)]
    d_full     <- d_excluding(dim_name)
    d_excluded <- d_excluding(dim_name, exclude_ids)

    # Where the observed post-exclusion d sits in the reference distribution.
    # `observed_percentile` is the share of matched random removals that
    # produced a d at or below the observed one. A value near 0.5 (the 50th
    # percentile) means the observed change is what removing a comparable set
    # of low raters produces.
    centre <- median(draws)
    tibble(
      set                 = set_label,
      dimension           = dim_name,
      effect_size         = "Cohen's d on participant means, pooled SD (Human - AI)",
      n_excluded          = n_drop,
      d_full_sample       = d_full,
      d_after_exclusion   = d_excluded,
      d_change            = d_excluded - d_full,
      null_median         = centre,
      null_ci_lo          = unname(quantile(draws, 0.025, names = FALSE)),
      null_ci_hi          = unname(quantile(draws, 0.975, names = FALSE)),
      observed_percentile = mean(draws <= d_excluded),
      p_two_sided         = mean(abs(draws - centre) >= abs(d_excluded - centre)),
      match_variable      = "participant mean effort rating",
      match_tolerance     = tol,
      target_mean_effort  = target,
      draws_accepted      = length(draws),
      draws_attempted     = attempts,
      acceptance_rate     = length(draws) / attempts
    )
  }))
}

leakage_placebo <- run_or_report(
  "5.5 matched random-removal comparison on the narrow set, 2,000 accepted draws",
  function() {
    key <- list(
      excluded = sort(belief_ids_narrow),
      means    = means_by_dimension,
      B        = B_BOOT,
      seed     = 20260421L,
      version  = "matched removal, effort-mean matching, both dimensions"
    )
    cached_or_run(MATCHED_CACHE_PATH, key, function() {
      matched_removal_null(belief_ids_narrow, "excluding the narrow set")
    })
  }
)

if (!is.null(leakage_placebo)) {
  glimpse(leakage_placebo)
  write_csv(leakage_placebo,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_leakage_placebo.csv"))
}
```

## 5.6 How to read the two numbers

```{r belief-audit-verdict}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The interpretation rule, stated in plain language and printed beside the
# numbers, because this pair of numbers is easy to misread.
#
# If the observed post-exclusion effect size sits INSIDE the matched
# distribution, then dropping these participants did nothing that dropping a
# random group with the same average effort rating would not have done. The
# change is what removing lower-rating people from the higher-rating arm
# produces, and it is not evidence about whether the manipulation was
# believed. In that case the rate in section 5.3 is the finding, and the
# change in effect size is not a finding at all.
#
# If it sits OUTSIDE, the result is not compatible with that reference, and
# it is reported as such without a story attached: the matching holds the
# average effort rating within a tolerance and nothing else, so it cannot say
# which other difference between the groups moved the effect size. The rate
# remains the reported quantity either way, because these are counts of what
# was written and not a manipulation check.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if (!is.null(leakage_placebo) &&
    "observed_percentile" %in% names(leakage_placebo)) {

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(leakage_placebo))) {
    row    <- leakage_placebo[i, ]
    inside <- row$d_after_exclusion >= row$null_ci_lo &
              row$d_after_exclusion <= row$null_ci_hi

    cat("\n", row$set, ", ", row$dimension, " ratings\n",
        "  Effect size, full sample:                d = ",
        sprintf("%.3f", row$d_full_sample), "\n",
        "  After dropping the ", row$n_excluded, " flagged participants: d = ",
        sprintf("%.3f", row$d_after_exclusion), "\n",
        "  Dropping a matched random set instead:   d = ",
        sprintf("%.3f", row$null_median),
        " (middle 95%: ", sprintf("%.3f", row$null_ci_lo),
        " to ", sprintf("%.3f", row$null_ci_hi), ")\n",
        "  The observed value sits at the ",
        sprintf("%.0f", 100 * row$observed_percentile),
        "th percentile of that distribution.\n", sep = "")

    if (isTRUE(inside)) {
      cat("  Reading: INSIDE the matched distribution. Removing a random\n",
          "  group with the same average effort rating moves the effect size\n",
          "  as far, so the change is not evidence about the manipulation.\n",
          "  Report the rate as the finding; do not report the effect-size\n",
          "  change as a manipulation check.\n", sep = "")
    } else {
      cat("  Reading: OUTSIDE the matched distribution. Removing these\n",
          "  participants left an effect size outside the range that removing\n",
          "  a random group with the same average effort rating produces, so\n",
          "  the change is not compatible with that reference. The matching holds\n",
          "  only the average effort rating, within a tolerance, so this does\n",
          "  not say why. The rate remains the reported quantity: these are\n",
          "  counts of what was written, not a manipulation check.\n",
          sep = "")
    }
  }

  cat("\nIn both cases the full-sample models in Study1_01_Quant.Rmd remain\n",
      "the primary analysis, and the excluded-sample estimate is never\n",
      "substituted for the primary one.\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{r prompt-by-arm}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 5 counted machine talk where it should not have appeared. This
# section reports it where it is expected, in the AI arm, so the two numbers
# can be read side by side and the leak rate has a scale to be judged against.

# Restricted to effort justifications, because that is where the process of
```

## 6.1 The same figures computed separately within each rating value

```{r prompt-by-arm-within-rating}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHY THIS BREAKDOWN EXISTS.
#
# The AI arm gives lower effort ratings, and the AI arm talks about prompting
# more. A sceptical reader can fairly ask whether the second fact is the
# first restated: whether "mentions prompting" stands in for "gave a low
# rating", in which case the arm difference in prompt talk carries
# no information beyond the rating difference already reported in
# Study1_01_Quant.Rmd.
#
# The test is to hold the rating fixed. Among the responses that gave effort a
# 1, what share in each arm mention prompting? Among the 2s? And so on. If the
# arm gap persists at every rating value, prompt talk is not a proxy for a low
# score: participants in the AI arm are reasoning about the production process
# even when they are giving the same number as someone in the human arm.
#
# Cells here can be small (few people give a 5 for effort in the AI arm), so
# each cell reports its own n, and a cell with fewer than 20 responses or
# fewer than 5 contributing participants gets no interval rather than an
# unreliable one.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c(
  "study1_text_prompt_by_arm_within_rating.csv",
  "study1_text_prompt_gap_within_rating.csv"
)))

MIN_CELL_N   <- 20L
MIN_CELL_IDS <- 5L

prompt_within_rating <- run_or_report(
  "6.1 prompt-talk rate by arm within each rating value",
  function() {
    cells <- effort_both_arms %>%
      filter(!is.na(rating)) %>%
      group_by(Type, rating) %>%
      summarise(
        n_responses    = n(),
        n_participants = n_distinct(id),
        rate_prompt    = mean(says_prompt),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    # Bootstrap each cell separately, resampling the participants who
    # contributed to that cell.
    ci <- cells %>%
      mutate(ci_lo = NA_real_, ci_hi = NA_real_, B = NA_integer_)

    for (i in seq_len(nrow(ci))) {
      if (ci$n_responses[i] < MIN_CELL_N ||
          ci$n_participants[i] < MIN_CELL_IDS) next
      sub <- effort_both_arms %>%
        filter(Type == ci$Type[i], rating == ci$rating[i])
      b <- boot_by_participant(
        sub,
        function(d) c(rate = mean(d$says_prompt)),
        seed = 20260421L + i
      )
      ci$ci_lo[i] <- b$ci_lo[1]
      ci$ci_hi[i] <- b$ci_hi[1]
      ci$B[i]     <- b$B[1]
    }

    ci %>%
      rename(arm = Type) %>%
      mutate(
        dimension = "effort",
        interval_reported = !is.na(ci_lo)
      ) %>%
      relocate(dimension, arm, rating)
  }
)

if (!is.null(prompt_within_rating)) {
  print(prompt_within_rating)
  write_csv(prompt_within_rating,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_prompt_by_arm_within_rating.csv"))

  # The arm gap at each rating value, in one column; this is the column to
  # read.
  gap <- prompt_within_rating %>%
    select(rating, arm, rate_prompt, n_responses) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = arm,
                values_from = c(rate_prompt, n_responses)) %>%
    mutate(gap_AI_minus_Human = rate_prompt_AI - rate_prompt_Human)
  print(gap)
  write_csv(gap, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                           "study1_text_prompt_gap_within_rating.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: whether gap_AI_minus_Human stays positive across rating
# values 1 through 5. If it does, the arm difference in prompt talk is not a
# restatement of the arm difference in ratings.
```

## 6.2 The fifth registered test: prompt talk across the machine arm's two dimensions

```{r prompt-dimension-test}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In the arm told an image generator made the work, prompting and generating
# words are plain description, and they answer a question of their own: what
# did those participants understand themselves to be rating? The
# preregistration predicts that prompt talk appears more often in that arm's
# effort explanations than in its creativity explanations: for someone who
# believes a machine made the picture, effort is partly a judgment about
# operating the machine.
#
#   says_prompt ~ dimension + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),  family = binomial
#
# fitted within the AI arm only, on both dimensions' justifications. This is
# the same mixed logistic regression as the four comparisons in 3.1.1 and
# 4.1.1, with the same random intercepts for participant and image; the one
# difference is that the predictor is the rating dimension rather than a
# stacked pair of flags, because here one flag is compared across the two
# questions rather than two flags within one. "creativity" is the reference
# level, so the `dimensioneffort` coefficient reads as the log-odds of prompt
# talk in an effort explanation minus the log-odds in a creativity
# explanation, from the same person at the same image, and a positive value
# is the predicted direction.
#
# The arm is fixed inside the function rather than passed in, because the
# preregistration fixes it.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
fit_prompt_dimension_test <- function(dat_x) {
  d <- dat_x %>%
    filter(Type == "AI") %>%
    mutate(
      dimension   = factor(as.character(dimension), levels = DIM_LEVELS),
      says_prompt = as.integer(says_prompt)
    )
  res <- fit_mixed(
    says_prompt ~ dimension + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), d,
    family = binomial,
    step = "registered text test: prompt talk, effort vs creativity"
  )
  row <- coef_row(res, "dimensioneffort") %>%
    mutate(
      comparison          = "prompt talk, effort vs creativity",
      arm                 = "AI",
      dimension           = "both",
      n_responses         = nrow(d),
      n_participants      = n_distinct(d$id),
      n_rows_stacked      = NA_integer_,
      rate_a              = mean(d$says_prompt[d$dimension == "effort"]),
      rate_b              = mean(d$says_prompt[d$dimension == "creativity"]),
      predicted_direction = "effort > creativity",
      observed_direction  = direction_words(estimate_log_odds,
                                            "effort", "creativity"),
      direction_as_predicted = !is.na(observed_direction) &
                               observed_direction == predicted_direction,
      model = paste0("says_prompt ~ dimension + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id), ",
                     "binomial, bobyqa"),
      note  = res$note
    ) %>%
    relocate(comparison, arm, dimension, n_responses, n_participants)
  list(row = row, fit = res$fit, data = d)
}

prompt_dimension_fit <- run_or_report(
  "6.2 prompt talk ~ dimension in the AI arm, mixed logistic regression",
  function() fit_prompt_dimension_test(dat)
)

prompt_dimension_test <- NULL
if (!is.null(prompt_dimension_fit)) {
  prompt_dimension_test <- prompt_dimension_fit$row
  prompt_dimension_test %>%
    select(comparison, arm, n_responses, n_participants, rate_a, rate_b,
           estimate_log_odds, se, z, p_raw, predicted_direction,
           observed_direction, note) %>%
    print(width = Inf)
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: the sign of estimate_log_odds (positive means prompt talk
# was more common in effort explanations than in creativity explanations for
# the same person at the same image), rate_a and rate_b for the two raw rates
# behind it, and the note. The corrected p-value is in section 7.
```

# 7. The five text tests as one family

The preregistration names five directional tests over the written explanations
(visible detail against time and against skill in the human arm's effort
explanations, concept against execution and against novelty in the human arm's
creativity explanations, and prompting talk across the machine arm's two rating
dimensions) and treats them as one exploratory family. This section brings the
five rows fitted in 3.1.1, 4.1.1 and 6.2 together, applies the registered
correction, and states the verdict.

## 7.1 The Benjamini-Hochberg correction and the verdict

```{r text-family-bh}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHY A CORRECTION, AND WHY THIS ONE.
#
# Five tests each read against .05 would, if nothing were going on, produce a
# false positive among them roughly one time in four. The registered remedy is
# the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure: sort the five p-values from smallest to
# largest, compare the k-th smallest against k/5 times .05, and call
# significant every test up to the largest k that passes. It holds the false
# discovery rate, the expected share of false positives among the tests
# called positive, at .05. That is a looser standard than the Holm
# procedure Study1_01_Quant.Rmd applies to the four confirmatory tests, which
# controls the chance of even one false positive across the whole family, and
# the looseness is deliberate: these five are exploratory, they are corrected
# as exploratory, and no result among them is offered in support of a
# prediction about the ratings. They are not added to the confirmatory
# family, and adding them would change the family the Holm correction was
# registered over.
#
# The family is always five. If one of the five fits failed, or finished with
# a status that does not permit inference (section 1.3), its row carries an
# empty p-value and the correction is still applied over n = 5, so a test
# that could not be run does not make the others easier to pass.
#
# The verdict for each test needs three things: a fit whose status is ok or
# singular, an observed direction that is the predicted one, and a corrected
# p-value below .05. A reliable difference in the wrong direction is reported
# as a reliable difference in the wrong direction, not as support.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_denotation_tests.csv"),
              file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_denotation_glmm_fits.rds"))

# The columns of the deposited table, in the order the preregistration's
# reporting commitment lists them.
FAMILY_COLS <- c("comparison", "arm", "dimension", "n_responses",
                 "n_participants", "estimate_log_odds", "se", "z", "p_raw",
                 "p_bh", "predicted_direction", "observed_direction", "note")

correct_text_family <- function(rows) {
  if (nrow(rows) != 5) {
    stop("Expected five rows in the text family and found ", nrow(rows),
         ". A section above did not produce its test.")
  }
  rows %>%
    mutate(p_bh = p.adjust(p_raw, method = "BH", n = 5L), .after = p_raw)
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  ifelse(is.na(x), "NA", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x))
}

text_family <- run_or_report(
  "7.1 the five text tests, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected as one family",
  function() {
    correct_text_family(bind_rows(denotation_effort_tests,
                                  denotation_creativity_tests,
                                  prompt_dimension_test))
  }
)

if (!is.null(text_family)) {
  text_family %>% select(all_of(FAMILY_COLS)) %>% print(width = Inf)
  write_csv(text_family %>% select(all_of(FAMILY_COLS)),
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_denotation_tests.csv"))

  # Save the five fitted models beside the other model objects, so a reviewer
  # can inspect a random-intercept variance or refit with a different
  # optimiser without re-running this file.
  saveRDS(
    c(lapply(effort_pair_fits, `[[`, "fit"),
      lapply(creativity_pair_fits, `[[`, "fit"),
      list(prompt_effort_vs_creativity = prompt_dimension_fit$fit)),
    file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_text_denotation_glmm_fits.rds")
  )

  # The verdict, in words, one line per test.
  cat("\nThe five text tests as one exploratory family ",
      "(Benjamini-Hochberg at .05):\n", sep = "")
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(text_family))) {
    r <- text_family[i, ]
    status <- if (!r$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS) {
      paste0("NO VERDICT: the fit's status is ", r$status,
             "; see the note column")
    } else if (is.na(r$p_bh)) {
      "NOT RUN; see the note column"
    } else if (r$p_bh < 0.05 && isTRUE(r$direction_as_predicted)) {
      "in the predicted direction and below .05 after correction"
    } else if (r$p_bh < 0.05) {
      "reliable, but in the OPPOSITE direction to the prediction"
    } else if (isTRUE(r$direction_as_predicted)) {
      "predicted direction, but not below .05 after correction"
    } else {
      "not in the predicted direction and not below .05 after correction"
    }
    cat("  ", sprintf("%-36s", r$comparison),
        " log-odds ", fmt_num(r$estimate_log_odds),
        " (SE ", fmt_num(r$se), "), p_raw ", fmt_num(r$p_raw, 4),
        ", p_bh ", fmt_num(r$p_bh, 4),
        "; predicted ", r$predicted_direction,
        ", observed ", ifelse(is.na(r$observed_direction), "NA",
                              r$observed_direction),
        "\n      -> ", status, "\n", sep = "")
  }
  n_supported <- sum(text_family$status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS &
                       text_family$p_bh < 0.05 &
                       text_family$direction_as_predicted, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat("\n", n_supported, " of the 5 tests are in the predicted direction ",
      "with p_bh below .05. These are exploratory and corrected as ",
      "exploratory; none is offered in support of a prediction about the ",
      "ratings, and none enters the confirmatory Holm family in ",
      "Study1_01_Quant.Rmd.\n", sep = "")
}
```

## 7.2 A sensitivity check on how the five models handle dependence

```{r text-family-slope-sensitivity}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THE REGISTERED MODEL ASSUMES, AND WHAT THIS CHECK RELAXES.
#
# Each of the five registered models gives every participant their own
# baseline rate of mentioning things, through the random intercept, but one
# shared gap between the two measures being compared. If participants differ
# in that gap (one person writes almost only about detail, another splits
# detail and time evenly), the registered model treats those differences as
# noise around a single gap, and its standard error can come out too small.
# The check is to let the gap vary by participant too, a random slope for
# the measure (or, in the fifth test, for the dimension):
#
#   flag ~ measure + (1 + measure | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),  family = binomial
#
# fitted to exactly the stacked rows each registered model saw. If the
# estimates and their standard errors barely move, the registered model's
# simpler dependence structure is not what carries the result.
#
# This is a sensitivity check and nothing more. It is not registered, it
# enters no correction family, and it changes no verdict in 7.1; the table
# sets each registered estimate beside its random-slope counterpart. A
# random-slope model asks more of the data, and a fit whose status does not
# permit inference keeps its estimate and loses its standard error and p.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                        "study1_text_denotation_slope_sensitivity.csv"))

slope_sensitivity <- run_or_report(
  "7.2 the five text tests with a participant random slope (sensitivity)",
  function() {
    pair_fits <- c(effort_pair_fits, creativity_pair_fits)
    pair_rows <- bind_rows(lapply(pair_fits, function(pf) {
      name_a <- levels(pf$stacked$measure)[2]
      res <- fit_mixed(
        flag ~ measure + (1 + measure | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
        pf$stacked, family = binomial,
        step = paste("7.2 random-slope sensitivity:", pf$row$comparison)
      )
      coef_row(res, paste0("measure", name_a)) %>%
        mutate(comparison = pf$row$comparison,
               model = paste0("flag ~ measure + (1 + measure | id) + ",
                              "(1 | stimulus_id), binomial, bobyqa"),
               note = res$note)
    }))
    prompt_res <- fit_mixed(
      says_prompt ~ dimension + (1 + dimension | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
      prompt_dimension_fit$data, family = binomial,
      step = "7.2 random-slope sensitivity: prompt talk, effort vs creativity"
    )
    prompt_row <- coef_row(prompt_res, "dimensioneffort") %>%
      mutate(comparison = prompt_dimension_test$comparison,
             model = paste0("says_prompt ~ dimension + (1 + dimension | id) ",
                            "+ (1 | stimulus_id), binomial, bobyqa"),
             note = prompt_res$note)
    bind_rows(pair_rows, prompt_row) %>%
      left_join(text_family %>%
                  select(comparison,
                         registered_estimate_log_odds = estimate_log_odds,
                         registered_se = se),
                by = "comparison") %>%
      mutate(role = "sensitivity check, not registered") %>%
      select(comparison, role, registered_estimate_log_odds, registered_se,
             estimate_log_odds, se, z, p_raw, status, model, note)
  }
)

if (!is.null(slope_sensitivity)) {
  slope_sensitivity %>%
    select(comparison, registered_estimate_log_odds, registered_se,
           estimate_log_odds, se, p_raw, status) %>%
    print(width = Inf)
  write_csv(slope_sensitivity,
            file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB,
                      "study1_text_denotation_slope_sensitivity.csv"))
}

# WHAT TO LOOK AT: whether estimate_log_odds sits close to the registered
# estimate, and how much larger se is than registered_se. Some growth in the
# standard error is the usual result, because the random-slope model does
# not treat every participant's gap as the same one.
```

---

# 8. Two checks run in every study

Sections 3 to 7 ask what the words meant. This section asks two questions
about the words that are put to every study in this program where a rating
exists, in the same form each time.

The first check asks how closely the words alone track the rating, and how
well they pick out the experimental arm. As a registered descriptive
quantity, it belongs to no correction family. It bears on why no text
measure in this project is read as a mechanism: a justification written with
the rating already chosen can carry information about the rating without
having produced it. For the arm it adds a question the stand-alone scores
cannot answer, namely whether the words tell the arms apart better than the
ratings already do. It answers that by setting a model of the arm on the
rating alone beside a model on the rating and the words together, both
scored on the same held-out participants (participants whose responses the
model was not fitted to).

The second check is the text version of the fourth registered prediction
about the ratings, which says that attributing the work to a machine makes a
rating more a property of the rater and less a property of the image. If that
is so, a participant told a machine made the works should reuse their own
words across the ten images more than a participant told a person did. The
check asks exactly that, in both dimensions, and states in advance that it
expects the machine arm to reuse more. Its two dimensions are corrected
together by the Holm procedure, set out in 8.2, and each is read as
supported, opposite direction or inconclusive.

For Study 1 the first check measures a quantity that is already partly
known. An earlier exploratory analysis of this same corpus measured how well
a different representation of each response (the lists of numbers described
in section 12) predicted the rating, and found that it predicted it closely.
The check below uses plain word counts and a registered procedure. For Study
1 it is reported as a re-measurement of a known quantity, not as a
prediction. The same exploratory analysis tried a version of the second
check built on those number lists. The arm difference it found did not
survive resampling participants, and section 12 records it as a null. The
word-overlap version below had not been run when it was first registered, on
7 September 2026. It was run later that month, and its test, its correction
and its three readings were settled in October 2026, after those estimates
had been read (section 9 of the preregistration document).

Four features of the code below are easy to miss, and each is explained
where it occurs. The five-response floor on the vocabulary is applied inside
each training fold (the participants a model is fitted on, section 8.1)
rather than to the whole corpus, so that held-out participants have no say
in which words enter the model. The shuffle that builds the reference for
the rating moves each participant's ratings only among that participant's
own explanations. The arm is modelled from the rating alone and from the
rating and the words together, so that what the words add to the rating can
be measured. The stranger baseline of the overlap check (how many words a
person shares with other people writing about the same image) is rebuilt
inside every bootstrap replicate, and the two dimensions are corrected
together by Holm. Section 9 of the preregistration document specifies all
four.

Both checks divide the work between the notebook and this file as sections 3
to 7 do. The notebook, blind to the arm and to the rating, writes
the count of each content word in each response, the list of those words, and
each response's set of distinct content words. This file joins the arm and the
rating to those tables and runs the statistics. None of the tables may carry
the arm, the rating or the text, and the reads below stop if one does.

## 8.1 How closely the words track the rating and the arm

```{r recoverability-read, message=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# THE WORD TABLES, AND THEIR CONTRACT.
#
# nlp/study1_text_wordcounts.csv has one row per response-word pair with a
# count above zero: id, stimulus_id, dimension, word, count. The words are
# content words, meaning lower-case runs of letters and apostrophes with the
# notebook's fixed list of function words (the, was, of, and the like)
# removed. The notebook keeps every word that appears in at least
# NOTEBOOK_MIN_RESPONSES (2) responses, and the registered floor of
# WORD_MIN_RESPONSES (5) is applied in 8.1 itself, inside each training fold.
# nlp/study1_text_vocabulary.csv lists the words the notebook kept with the
# number of responses each appears in.
#
# Neither file may carry the arm, the rating, the text or the condition. The
# check is the same shape as the flags contract in section 2.3: the forbidden
# columns named explicitly first, so that the assertion reads as a blind check
# to anyone skimming, then nothing missing and nothing extra. The same helper
# checks every other table sections 8 and 9 read.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NOTEBOOK_MIN_RESPONSES <- 2L
WORD_MIN_RESPONSES     <- 5L

WORDCOUNT_COLS   <- c("id", "stimulus_id", "dimension", "word", "count")
VOCABULARY_COLS  <- c("word", "n_responses")
TOKENS_COLS      <- c("id", "stimulus_id", "dimension", "content_words")
AFFECT_COLS      <- c("id", "stimulus_id", "dimension", "n_content_words",
                      "n_vad_matched", "valence", "arousal", "dominance",
                      "n_conc_matched", "concreteness")
TOPICS_COLS      <- c("id", "stimulus_id", "dimension", "topic", "weight")
TOPIC_WORDS_COLS <- c("dimension", "topic", "rank", "word", "weight")

check_blind_columns <- function(m, expected, label) {
  present <- intersect(FORBIDDEN_COLS, names(m))
  if (length(present) > 0) {
    stop("BLIND BROKEN: ", label, " contains ", paste(present, collapse = ", "),
         ". The text tables may carry neither the condition, nor the rating, ",
         "nor the text. Fix Study1_02_Text.ipynb.")
  }
  missing_cols <- setdiff(expected, names(m))
  extra_cols   <- setdiff(names(m), expected)
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(label, " is missing required columns: ",
         paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (length(extra_cols) > 0) {
    stop(label, " has columns it should not have: ",
         paste(extra_cols, collapse = ", "))
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# A table with one row per response must name exactly the responses the
# ratings file names, no more and no fewer.
check_response_keys <- function(m, label) {
  keys_m <- paste(m$id, m$stimulus_id, m$dimension)
  keys_r <- paste(ratings$id, ratings$stimulus_id, ratings$dimension)
  if (anyDuplicated(keys_m) > 0) {
    stop(label, " has more than one row for some response.")
  }
  if (!setequal(keys_m, keys_r)) {
    stop(label, " and the ratings file name different sets of responses (",
```
