## 10.2 The ten images: detail talk against average effort rating

```{r fig-detail-scatter-helper}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A small labelling helper, defined before the plot that uses it. It labels
# each point with its image name, using the ggrepel package if that package
# happens to be installed (ggrepel nudges labels apart so they do not overlap)
# and plain text if it is not. Written this way so the file does not
# hard-depend on ggrepel: the figure is identical in content either way.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
label_points <- function(d) {
  if (requireNamespace("ggrepel", quietly = TRUE)) {
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      data = d, aes(label = stimulus_id),
      size = 2.7, color = "grey25", seed = 20260421,
      min.segment.length = 0.2, box.padding = 0.35
    )
  } else {
    geom_text(data = d, aes(label = stimulus_id),
              size = 2.7, color = "grey25",
              vjust = -0.9, check_overlap = TRUE)
  }
}
```

```{r fig-detail-scatter, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each point is one artwork. Horizontal position: the share of that image's
# effort justifications that mentioned visible detail. Vertical position: that
# image's average effort rating. Both computed in the human-attribution arm
# only, matching section 3.3.
#
# Point shape distinguishes the two stimulus families (figure-containing vs.
# not), because a reader will want to check that any relationship is not just
# the five figures sitting apart from the five non-figures.
#
# The dashed line is an ordinary straight-line fit through the ten points,
# shown for orientation only. No shaded band is drawn around it: a regression
# band here would be computed as though the ten images were ten independent
# observations, which would understate the uncertainty. The interval to quote
# is the participant-resampled one from section 3.3, printed in the subtitle.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, c("study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.pdf",
                                        "study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.png")),
              file.path(PATH_PAPER_FIG, "study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.pdf"))

fig_detail_scatter <- run_or_report("10.2 image scatter", function() {

  r_label <- if (!is.null(image_corr)) {
    sprintf("r = %.2f  [%.2f, %.2f]",
            image_corr$estimate[1], image_corr$ci_lo[1], image_corr$ci_hi[1])
  } else NULL

  ggplot(image_stats, aes(x = detail_rate, y = mean_effort)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
                color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(aes(shape = stimulus_type), size = 3, color = "#3E3E3E",
               fill = "#A1A1A1", stroke = 0.6) +
    label_points(image_stats) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("NonFigure" = 21, "Figure" = 24),
                       name = "Stimulus type") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                       expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 5), breaks = 1:5) +
    labs(
      x        = "Share of effort justifications mentioning visible detail",
      y        = "Mean effort rating (1-5)",
      subtitle = if (!is.null(r_label))
                   paste0("Human-attribution arm, ten images; ", r_label,
                          " (95% interval from resampling participants)")
                 else "Human-attribution arm, ten images"
    ) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.subtitle     = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "grey30"),
      legend.position   = "right",
      legend.background = element_blank(),
      axis.text         = element_text(color = "black")
    )
})

if (!is.null(fig_detail_scatter)) {
  print(fig_detail_scatter)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, "study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.pdf"),
         fig_detail_scatter, width = 6.5, height = 4.8, device = cairo_pdf)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, "study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.png"),
         fig_detail_scatter, width = 6.5, height = 4.8, dpi = 300)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_PAPER_FIG, "study1_fig4_detail_vs_effort.pdf"),
         fig_detail_scatter, width = 6.5, height = 4.8, device = cairo_pdf)
}
```

## 10.3 The two denotation profiles side by side

```{r fig-denotation-profiles, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.2}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The figure the argument in sections 3 and 4 turns on: what each of the two
# rated words was about, drawn on one shared vertical scale so the profiles
# can be compared by eye instead of across two tables.
#
# Left panel, the three candidate meanings of "effort" from section 3.1.
# Right panel, the three candidate meanings of "creativity" from section 4.1.
# Both are shares of justifications in the human-attribution arm, on the same
# vertical scale, with the same participant-resampled 95% intervals computed
# earlier. Nothing is recomputed here; the bars are the numbers already written
# to study1_text_effort_prevalence.csv and study1_text_creativity_prevalence.csv.
#
# Novelty is shown as a single bar (the share of creativity justifications in
# which novelty was raised at all, in either direction), because the other two
# bars in that panel are also single yes/no measures, and splitting only one
# of them into asserted and negated would make the panel a comparison of
# unlike things. The asserted/negated split is in the table and in section
# 4.3, where the direction is the point.
#
# Greyscale throughout, matching Study1_01_Quant.Rmd: a single neutral fill,
# black error bars, no colour carrying any information.
#
# WHAT TO LOOK AT: whether the tallest bar in the right panel is concept talk
# or execution talk, and how the right panel's shape compares with the left.
# Two profiles that look alike would mean the raters were describing much the
# same property twice under two names, which is the reading the paper has to be
# able to rule out before it can treat creativity and effort as the separate
# constructs Feist treats them as.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, c("study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.pdf",
                                        "study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.png")),
              file.path(PATH_PAPER_FIG, "study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.pdf"))

fig_denotation <- run_or_report("10.3 denotation comparison figure", function() {

  stopifnot(!is.null(effort_prevalence), !is.null(creativity_prevalence))

  # The six bars, in the order they should be drawn. Building one long table
  # first, rather than two plots, guarantees both panels share a scale.
  profile_dat <- bind_rows(
    effort_prevalence %>%
      filter(quantity %in% c("detail", "time", "skill")) %>%
      mutate(label = recode(quantity,
                            detail = "Detail talk",
                            time   = "Time talk",
                            skill  = "Skill talk"),
             panel = "What \"effort\" was about"),
    creativity_prevalence %>%
      filter(quantity %in% c("concept", "novelty_either", "execution")) %>%
      mutate(label = recode(quantity,
                            concept        = "Concept talk",
                            novelty_either = "Novelty talk",
                            execution      = "Execution talk"),
             panel = "What \"creativity\" was about")
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      label = factor(label, levels = c("Detail talk", "Time talk",
                                       "Skill talk", "Concept talk",
                                       "Novelty talk", "Execution talk")),
      panel = factor(panel, levels = c("What \"effort\" was about",
                                       "What \"creativity\" was about"))
    )

  ggplot(profile_dat, aes(x = label, y = estimate)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.62, fill = FILL_NEUTRAL) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi),
                  width = 0.14, linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
    # scales = "free_x" gives each panel only its own three categories; the
    # vertical scale stays shared, which is the point of the figure.
    facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))) +
    labs(
      x        = NULL,
      y        = "Share of justifications",
      title    = "What each rated word denoted",
      subtitle = paste0("Human-attribution arm; categories are not mutually ",
                        "exclusive; 95% intervals from resampling participants")
    ) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "grey30"),
      strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5),
      strip.background = element_blank(),
      axis.text     = element_text(color = "black"),
      panel.spacing = unit(1.1, "lines")
    )
})

if (!is.null(fig_denotation)) {
  print(fig_denotation)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, "study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.pdf"),
         fig_denotation, width = 7.5, height = 4.2, device = cairo_pdf)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_OUT_FIG, "study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.png"),
         fig_denotation, width = 7.5, height = 4.2, dpi = 300)
  ggsave(file.path(PATH_PAPER_FIG, "study1_fig5_denotation_profiles.pdf"),
         fig_denotation, width = 7.5, height = 4.2, device = cairo_pdf)
}
```

# 11. Run record and session information

## 11.1 Did anything fail?

```{r model-log}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two logs, written side by side. MODEL_LOG has one row per wrapped step,
# with the status "ok" or "error"; an "error" row means the step's outputs
# were not written this run (section 1.4 deleted them before the step ran),
# and any number the manuscript cites from them has no current source.
# FIT_LOG has one row per mixed model fitted anywhere in this file, with the
# status of section 1.3 (ok, singular, nonconvergence or error) and its note;
# a nonconvergence or error row is a model whose p-value, interval and
# verdict are NA in its table. Check both before quoting anything.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_text_model_log.csv",
                                        "study1_text_fit_log.csv")))

MODEL_LOG
write_csv(MODEL_LOG, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_model_log.csv"))
write_csv(FIT_LOG %>% mutate(run_id = RUN_ID, .before = 1),
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_fit_log.csv"))

n_failed <- sum(MODEL_LOG$status == "error")
if (n_failed > 0) {
  cat("\n", n_failed, " step(s) failed. See the table above.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("\nAll steps completed.\n")
}
print(FIT_LOG %>% count(status, name = "n_fits"))
not_eligible <- FIT_LOG %>% filter(!status %in% ELIGIBLE_STATUS)
if (nrow(not_eligible) > 0) {
  cat("\nFits whose status does not permit inference:\n")
  print(not_eligible %>% select(step, status, note), n = Inf, width = Inf)
} else {
  cat("Every mixed model finished with status ok or singular.\n")
}
```

```{r manifest}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two manifests, both built from the paths registered through clear_outputs()
# rather than typed out by hand, so they cannot drift out of date.
#
# tables/study1_text_manifest.csv lists every output with whether it exists,
# its size and its modification time, and written_this_run beside them.
#
# tables/study1_integration_run_manifest.csv is the run record the
# downstream files check. One row per input, with role "input", status
# "read" and its SHA-256 checksum; then one row per output, with role
# "output", status "written" when this run wrote it and "not written"
# otherwise, written_this_run, its size and its checksum. written_this_run is
# TRUE when the file exists and its modification time is no earlier than the
# second in which this run started; every listed output was deleted at the
# top of the chunk that writes it, so FALSE means that chunk wrote nothing.
# The run manifest is written last and does not list itself; because the
# previous one is deleted when the run starts, a run manifest on disk means
# the run reached this chunk.
#
# The matched-removal cache in models/ is not listed: it is a working file
# that section 5.5 rebuilds whenever its key stops matching, not a result.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_manifest.csv"))

manifest_label <- function(p) {
  if (startsWith(p, paste0(PATH_OUT, "/"))) {
    return(substring(p, nchar(PATH_OUT) + 2))
  }
  if (startsWith(p, paste0(PATH_PAPER, "/"))) {
    return(file.path("Docs", "Writing", "Final Paper",
                     substring(p, nchar(PATH_PAPER) + 2)))
  }
  p
}

run_start_sec <- trunc(RUN_START, units = "secs")
written_now <- function(paths) {
  ex <- file.exists(paths)
  coalesce(ex & file.mtime(paths) >= run_start_sec, FALSE)
}

# The text manifest is written before the run manifest is computed, so that
# the run manifest can record it too.
listed <- setdiff(INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS,
                  c(PATH_RUN_MANIFEST,
                    file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_manifest.csv")))
manifest <- tibble(
  file             = vapply(listed, manifest_label, character(1),
                            USE.NAMES = FALSE),
  exists           = file.exists(listed),
  size_kb          = ifelse(file.exists(listed),
                            round(file.size(listed) / 1024, 1), NA_real_),
  modified         = as.character(file.mtime(listed)),
  written_this_run = written_now(listed)
)
manifest %>% print(n = Inf)
write_csv(manifest, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_text_manifest.csv"))

out_paths <- setdiff(INTEGRATION_OUTPUTS, PATH_RUN_MANIFEST)
out_exist <- file.exists(out_paths)
out_now   <- written_now(out_paths)
run_manifest <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    run_id           = RUN_ID,
    stage            = "integration",
    role             = "input",
    file             = vapply(unname(INPUT_FILES), manifest_label, character(1)),
    status           = "read",
    written_this_run = FALSE,
    bytes            = unname(file.size(INPUT_FILES)),
    sha256           = INPUT_SHA256
  ),
  tibble(
    run_id           = RUN_ID,
    stage            = "integration",
    role             = "output",
    file             = vapply(out_paths, manifest_label, character(1),
                              USE.NAMES = FALSE),
    status           = ifelse(out_now, "written", "not written"),
    written_this_run = out_now,
    bytes            = ifelse(out_exist, file.size(out_paths), NA_real_),
    sha256           = ifelse(out_exist, unname(tools::sha256sum(out_paths)),
                              NA_character_)
  )
)

cat("Outputs listed:", sum(run_manifest$role == "output"),
    "| written this run:", sum(run_manifest$written_this_run),
    "| not written:", sum(run_manifest$role == "output" &
                            !run_manifest$written_this_run), "\n")
if (any(run_manifest$role == "output" & !run_manifest$written_this_run)) {
  cat("Not written this run:\n")
  print(run_manifest$file[run_manifest$role == "output" &
                            !run_manifest$written_this_run])
}
write_csv(run_manifest, PATH_RUN_MANIFEST)
```

# 12. Approaches that were tested and did not work

This section records approaches that were tried on this corpus and set
aside, so that they are not tried again. Each entry says what was tried and
why it was set aside.

**Turning each response into a list of numbers and clustering them.** A
sentence can be converted into a few hundred numbers that place it in a space
where similar sentences sit near each other, and those positions can be
grouped into clusters. On this corpus the clusters were unstable (small
changes to the settings produced different groupings) and, more importantly,
nobody could state in advance what any cluster would contain. A measure that
cannot be written down before it is applied cannot be audited, and every count
it produced would have rested on the analyst's judgment after seeing the data.

**Asking a language model to label each response.** This is fast and its
labels read well, but it puts a judgment call inside every count, and the
judgments cannot be reproduced exactly by anyone else or checked against a
printed rule. In this program researcher judgment enters once, in the rules,
and every match can be traced to the phrase that triggered it.

**Using sentiment as a measure of what a word meant.** The justifications are
short and evaluative by construction, since every one of them is explaining a
rating, so a sentiment score tracked the rating almost perfectly and could not
say what the rated word denoted. Sentiment is therefore not one of the
measures of sections 3 to 7. Section 9.1 reports the valence of the words, from
published norms, as a description of the vocabulary with the rating held in
the model, and draws no conclusion about meaning from it.

**Topic models over the whole corpus at once.** With a median of
`r corpus_check$words_median` words per response
(`r corpus_by_dim$words_median[corpus_by_dim$dimension == "creativity"]` in
creativity explanations,
`r corpus_by_dim$words_median[corpus_by_dim$dimension == "effort"]` in effort
explanations), a topic model fitted to both dimensions' explanations at once
found topics dominated by the rating scale's own wording, the wording the
`anchor_echo` flag marks, and could not stand in for the fixed rules. The
topic description of section 9.2 is a different procedure: it is fitted to
each dimension separately, with the rating questions' own words removed, and
its number of topics is set by a stability rule written into the notebook. It
is reported as description and is not a measure any test rests on.

**Using the number-lists themselves as measures.** The same conversion of a
response into a list of numbers can be used directly, by asking how well those
numbers predict the rating the response accompanied. On this corpus they predict
it closely, on both dimensions. That is not a success for the purpose of this
file. A text measure built to track the rating cannot by that fact say what the
person meant by the word they used, which is the only question this file asks
the text. Such a measure is set aside as a measure. It remains admissible in a
later study only if it answers a question no word list can, holds after the
rating is controlled for, and survives resampling participants.

**Re-deriving the variance result from how alike each person's sentences are.**
If a participant under machine attribution gives the same number to every image,
one might expect that participant's ten explanations to resemble each other more
than a human-arm participant's do, and the number-lists make that resemblance
measurable. The difference between arms was in the predicted direction on the
observed sample and did not survive resampling participants: the interval on the
arm difference included zero. It is recorded here as a null, so that the claim is
not re-made from the same data.

**Reading who is the grammatical subject of the making verb.** During
development a grammar-based rule was built: one that reads the structure of a
sentence to find whether the artist, the tool, or no one is the subject of
the verb describing how the work was made. It fired on about a quarter of
responses. It was not validated and is not used anywhere in the pipeline. Its
working files, in `nlp/agency_rule_candidates`, are side work kept outside the
published pipeline.

1. `Study1_01_Quant.Rmd`, which writes `study1_long_with_text.csv`.
2. `Study1_02_Text.ipynb`, which writes `nlp/study1_text_measures.csv`, the
   tables sections 8 and 9 read (`nlp/study1_text_wordcounts.csv`,
   `nlp/study1_text_vocabulary.csv`, `nlp/study1_text_tokens.csv`,
   `nlp/study1_text_affect.csv`, `nlp/study1_text_topics.csv` and
   `tables/text_topics_top_words.csv`), plus the rules with their checksum and
   grounding notes, the audit, the candidate-word list, the keyness tables,
   the topic-stability tables and the corpus summary in `tables/`.
3. This file.
